speechtext: On the orders of the day:

speakeroldname: Right Hon. J. G. Diefenbaker (Prime Minister):
maintopic: ATOMIC ENERGY
subtopic: STATEMENT ON CONSTRUCTION OF PLANT AT MONROE, MICHIGAN
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the hon. member for Essex West asked me a question as to whether or not a report requested by the U.A.W. international union on the construction of an atomic energy plant at Monroe, Michigan, had been received and, if so, was I satisfied that the public safety is assured.
The reactor referred to is a large power reactor being built on the shore of lake Erie near Monroe, Michigan. A permit for the construction of this reactor was issued by the United States atomic energy commission in August of 1956. The commission pointed out, however, that the permit was conditional since the design details were not final, and it emphasized that a licence for operation would not be granted until the commission was satisfied as to the safety of the reactor. Later, as a result of opposition to the construction permit, the commission scheduled public hearings on the safety aspects of the reactor. These hearings have recently been completed and as yet no decision has been announced by the commission.
The Canadian government, through the atomic energy control board, has been following this project closely since its inception. Information has been obtained from the atomic energy commission, and Canadian representatives have attended the public hearings in Washington. The board's advisers have pointed out that there is no hazard in construction operations, and they are of the opinion that a reactor of the contemplated type can be designed so as to be capable of safe operation. They have pointed out, however, that until details of the final design are available a full assessment of the safety of this project is not possible.

Inquiries of the Ministry
Representations have been made to the United States government setting out the interest of the Canadian government in this matter and its desire to be kept informed of the progress in the design of this reactor. Further representations will be made if it appears that operation might result in a hazard to the Canadian public.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would like to address a question to the Postmaster General. I do wish he would continue to wear his bright red waistcoat. When he does we can see him easily, and we consider it a symbol of the parliamentary mail box into which we can drop inquiries. Incidentally, Mr. Speaker, we also consider it a touch of colour in the otherwise vulpine Victorian vista opposite. Now for my question.
In view of the numerous protests from philatelists, more commonly known as stamp collectors, concerning the alleged elimination of plate numbers from further issues of stamps, and since because the minister's estimates were passed by the last parliament we are denied the normal opportunity to interrogate or irritate the minister, or the minister the opportunity to reply, would the minister under these circumstances make a statement concerning the procedures of the philatelic branch of his department, for the information of the house and the country, having regard to and being guided by memories of his relentless quest for complete information on postal affairs when a member of the opposition?

maintopic: POST OFFICE DEPARTMENT
subtopic: REQUEST FOR STATEMENT ON PRACTICE OF PHILATELIC BRANCH
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I do feel that under normal circumstances this would be a question better dealt with on the estimates. As the hon. member has pointed out, my estimates will not be before the house this year; therefore with your permission I might just say a word or two in reply to the question. I want first to thank my hon. friend for having given me notice of this subject.


The hon. member referred to numerous protests from philatelists regarding this situation. I might say we have also had commendation from philatelists. The house will remember that by action of the last government plate numbers on stamps were eliminated. When we studied the situation it became apparent that philatelists were very desirous of having these plate numbers included on the sheets, and we sought a way in which they could be made available to them.
This was accomplished by continuing the printing of these plate numbers on the margins of sheets of stamps but cutting them off the sheets which were designed for ordinary sale in post offices across Canada, thus eliminating delays and confusion at stamp wickets which had brought criticism from the public in the past. However, these same stamps, printed from exactly the same plates, in every way identical but with the plate block numbers left on, are available to philatelists through the philatelic section here in Ottawa under exactly the same conditions as have prevailed for a number of years in the past. The philatelic section to which the hon. member makes reference has been designed and devoted completely to the convenience and assistance of philatelists in obtaining the desired stamps directly from the post office.
One further point on which comment has been made has been the question of deposits. I might emphasize the fact that the philatelic section sells these stamps at their face value without any deposit whatsoever being required. There is a deposit system for those who wish automatic forwarding of new stamps as they are issued, but that is not a requirement to buy from the philatelic section.
I think that would cover the ground which interests the hon. member, Mr. Speaker.

speechtext:
Yesterday the hon. member for Bow River asked the following question:
According to press reports 82 men were laid off at one of the mines in Drumheller last week, and one of the large mines in Canmore is closing because of lack of orders. Can the minister tell the house what plans the government has in mind for increasing the markets for coal so the distressed coal industry of Alberta may get some relief?
It is my understanding that the press report in regard to the shutting down of one of the mines at Drumheller is correct. The combination of surplus oil and gas with an unusually mild fall and winter has reduced consumption of domestic coal and has produced, at an unusually early time, the condition of seasonal surplus which has been chronic in this field. These seasonal fluctuations in supply and demand have been matters that are not amenable to any control by government.
In respect to the report of the mine at Canmore, the subvention assistance provided by government enabled this mine to maintain operations last year and the present position is at this time under sympathetic study by the dominion coal board, who have met with the mine operators and whose full membership are now in session in Ottawa. It is my opinion that the report of closing is premature, and that the government will be able to forestall a shut-down by accepting the recommendations of the board.

Special classes of this nature have been operating in British Columbia, Alberta, Saskatchewan and Manitoba during the past three years, and the costs of such training have been shared equally with the provincial governments under the provisions of schedule M of the vocational training agreement, as authorized by the Vocational Training Coordination Act.
The primary reason for establishing such classes was to provide suitable work for unemployed Canadians and at the same time avoid the necessity of continuing to import pipe-line welders from the United States. maintopic: DOMINION-PROVINCIAL RELATIONS MEASURE TO PROVIDE FINANCIAL ASSISTANCE TO ATLANTIC PROVINCES, ETC.

speechtext:
The house resumed, from Monday, January 27, consideration in committee of the following resolution-Mr. Fleming-Mr. Courte-manche in the chair:
That it is expedient to introduce a measure to provide for financial assistance to the Atlantic provinces by authorizing the payment, out of the consolidated revenue fund, for each of the four fiscal years commencing on the first day of April, 1958, of an annual grant of seven and one-half million dollars to each of the provinces of Nova Scotia, New Brunswick and Newfoundland, and an annual grant of two and one-half million dollars to the province of Prince Edward Island, and also to provide as an interim measure that in its application to the fiscal year commencing on the first day of April, 1958, the definition of "standard individual income tax'' in the Federal-Provincial Tax-Sharing Arrangements Act, shall for the purposes of that act and any agreements made thereunder be read and construed as if for the words "10 per cent" therein there were substituted the words "13 per cent".

maintopic: DOMINION-PROVINCIAL RELATIONS MEASURE TO PROVIDE FINANCIAL ASSISTANCE TO ATLANTIC PROVINCES, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, on Saturday the Minister of Finance when tabling the telegram which had been sent by the Prime Minister to the premiers of the 10 provinces indicated-and this can be found on page 3795 of Hansard-indicated how the sum of money mentioned in the telegrams would be divided among the provinces in the fiscal year commencing April 1. Yesterday he had a table printed in Hansard also giving the distribution of this amount between the various provinces, and this table can be found at page 3850 of Hansard for yesterday.
I cannot understand how there could be such variation between the figures the Minister of Finance mentioned on Saturday and those he indicated yesterday. For instance, on Saturday Prince Edward Island was led
[Mr. Hamilton (Qu'Appelle) .1
to believe that apart from the special Atlantic provinces grant it would receive an additional $370,000 as an increase under the fiscal arrangements. According to the figures tabled yesterday, which can be found, as I said, at page 3850 of Hansard, the increase for Prince Edward Island has completely disappeared.
In the case of British Columbia, the Minister of Finance announced on Saturday an increase of $5,563,000; but according to the figures produced yesterday this amount has decreased to $2,842,000. The total amount of the increase, $62 million, remained approximately the same on Monday as it was on Saturday, but with Quebec and Ontario each getting approximately $1 million more than was announced on Saturday.
I ask the Minister of Finance how Saturday's figures were prepared. How was it possible to mislead provincial premiers to such an extent, especially those of British Columbia and Prince Edward Island? Was it in order to get a better press throughout the country so it would be known that all provinces without exception would benefit from this new deal? Who did the arithmetic for Saturday's figures? Was it the Minister of Finance alone, or was he helped by his officials? What faith can the country have in a minister of finance who at an interval of only two days announces to this house and to the country two different sets of figures without explanation-

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: DOMINION-PROVINCIAL RELATIONS MEASURE TO PROVIDE FINANCIAL ASSISTANCE TO ATLANTIC PROVINCES, ETC.
speechtext: The explanation was given yesterday, but you were not here to hear it.

maintopic: DOMINION-PROVINCIAL RELATIONS MEASURE TO PROVIDE FINANCIAL ASSISTANCE TO ATLANTIC PROVINCES, ETC.
speechtext:
I am going to deal with that explanation, and show how weak it is. We know, of course, that on Saturday the Minister of Finance had forgotten the stabilization payments being received in 1957 and 1958 by British Columbia and Prince Edward Island. But how could he forget those payments? I am afraid he was in such a hurry to try to obtain political advantage that he was not prepared on Saturday, as he was not prepared at Mont Tremblant. He has not done his home work, at the risk of misleading the provincial governments and the country as a whole.
As to the variation in the figures between Saturday and yesterday for the other eight provinces, what explanation has the minister given?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: DOMINION-PROVINCIAL RELATIONS MEASURE TO PROVIDE FINANCIAL ASSISTANCE TO ATLANTIC PROVINCES, ETC.
speechtext: I gave it twice yesterday. Apparently you were not here.

maintopic: DOMINION-PROVINCIAL RELATIONS MEASURE TO PROVIDE FINANCIAL ASSISTANCE TO ATLANTIC PROVINCES, ETC.
speechtext:
I will quote that explanation from page 3874 of Hansard. Answering a question put to him by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre the minister had this to say:
The other eight provinces receive benefit from the fact that British Columbia and Prince Edward

Island do not now take their full share byreason of the prior application of the stabilization principle.
That is not a satisfactory answer. It is not and it cannot be the explanation.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: DOMINION-PROVINCIAL RELATIONS MEASURE TO PROVIDE FINANCIAL ASSISTANCE TO ATLANTIC PROVINCES, ETC.
speechtext: It is.

maintopic: DOMINION-PROVINCIAL RELATIONS MEASURE TO PROVIDE FINANCIAL ASSISTANCE TO ATLANTIC PROVINCES, ETC.
speechtext: I fail to see how the fact that British Columbia and Prince Edward Island are receiving stabilization payments during the present fiscal year can have any effect on the amounts to be paid to the other provinces in the next fiscal year. The basis of the present fiscal arrangements is not the distribution of a set or given amount. It is not a fixed amount.

maintopic: DOMINION-PROVINCIAL RELATIONS MEASURE TO PROVIDE FINANCIAL ASSISTANCE TO ATLANTIC PROVINCES, ETC.
speechtext:
He
does not know that.

maintopic: DOMINION-PROVINCIAL RELATIONS MEASURE TO PROVIDE FINANCIAL ASSISTANCE TO ATLANTIC PROVINCES, ETC.
speechtext:
Similarly, and leaving aside the special grants for the Atlantic provinces, the proposed increases in the fiscal payments to the provinces which are indicated under this resolution are not based on the distribution of a set, fixed or given amount of $62 million.
I have made calculations of my own from the table printed in Hansard yesterday. If you divide the amount of the increase for each province, less the special grants for the Atlantic provinces, by the figure of the population of each province, you arrive in each case at a figure of approximately $3.97 which seems to me-and I want to be corrected if I am wrong-to represent the estimated average yield in 1957-58 in the two so-called top provinces-Ontario and British Columbia-of 3 per cent of the federal income tax per head of population.
I should like the Minister of Finance to correct me if I am wrong, and to tell the committee what exactly is the estimated average yield in the two top provinces of 3 per cent of personal income taxes in 1957-58 per head of population.
In the table which was printed in Hansard yesterday there are two exceptions, British Columbia and Prince Edward Island. I have mentioned these already. But in the case of British Columbia, if you add to the total increase of $2,842,000 the stabilization payment of $3,046,000 you arrive at the same figure of approximately $3.97 per head of population.
This sum of $3.97 per head in each province of Canada is the increase that is proposed by this resolution, an increase which amounts to one cent a day per head of population across Canada. That is one cent a day per head of population in each province. Is that the great new deal which was offered during the election by the Tories to the provincial governments? Yes, that is the
Dominion-Provincial Relations great new deal imposed upon the provinces by a telegram from the Prime Minister.
According to other calculations I have made, of the $18.8 million increase that would go to Quebec, $5.7 million would go to the provincial government as equalization payment. I stand to be corrected, and I would like the Minister of Finance to correct me if I am wrong.

maintopic: DOMINION-PROVINCIAL RELATIONS MEASURE TO PROVIDE FINANCIAL ASSISTANCE TO ATLANTIC PROVINCES, ETC.
speechtext: His officials are not here.

maintopic: DOMINION-PROVINCIAL RELATIONS MEASURE TO PROVIDE FINANCIAL ASSISTANCE TO ATLANTIC PROVINCES, ETC.
speechtext:
The amount of $5.7 million would go to the provincial government as equalization payments, and the taxpayers who are subject to double taxation would be partially relieved to the extent of $13.1 million. Now, this 13 per cent reduction in the federal rates will take effect on April 1,
1958.	It will have its effect for nine months of the year 1958; but the taxpayers of Canada and of course those who live in Quebec will be filing their income tax returns for the whole of the calendar year 1958. Does this mean that the reduction to be allowed to taxpayers for 1958 will be the existing 10 per cent plus 75 per cent of the additional 3 per cent, that is to say 12J per cent, for the year 1958? That, of course, will not make any easier the preparation of income tax returns.
And what about 1959? After all, the increase will be valid only until April 1, 1959. Thus the reduction for Quebec taxpayers in 1959 instead of being 12J per cent will be only 10.75 per cent for the whole of the year
1959.	What is the answer to that problem? How is this going to work? This is the kind of result one achieves when he tampers on an interim basis with well established policy.
I have another question, this time about the stabilization angle. On July 16, 1956, the then minister of finance, Mr. Harris, as recorded at page 5990 of Hansard of that date, said when presenting the resolution to give effect to the present arrangements:
-the bill will provide for:-(4) a provincial revenue stabilization payment to any province when the yield of the present proposal falls below certain floors
Of course the guarantee at that time was based on the yield at the standard rates, and for personal income tax it was 10 per cent. My question to the present Minister of Finance is this. Will the guarantee be amended as if the standard rate of the personal income tax for 1957-58 had been 13 per cent? This is important, because a decline in the yield of direct taxes in 1958-59 coupled with the reductions in income tax announced by the Minister of Finance in December would have the effect of decreasing, possibly

Dominion-Provincial Relations to a substantial degree, the benefits the provinces could derive from the proposed measure.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: DOMINION-PROVINCIAL RELATIONS MEASURE TO PROVIDE FINANCIAL ASSISTANCE TO ATLANTIC PROVINCES, ETC.
speechtext: That point was dealt with yesterday in my remarks.

maintopic: DOMINION-PROVINCIAL RELATIONS MEASURE TO PROVIDE FINANCIAL ASSISTANCE TO ATLANTIC PROVINCES, ETC.
speechtext: No, it was not. I checked Hansard very carefully, and I find it was not dealt with.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: DOMINION-PROVINCIAL RELATIONS MEASURE TO PROVIDE FINANCIAL ASSISTANCE TO ATLANTIC PROVINCES, ETC.
speechtext: You had better read it again.

maintopic: DOMINION-PROVINCIAL RELATIONS MEASURE TO PROVIDE FINANCIAL ASSISTANCE TO ATLANTIC PROVINCES, ETC.
speechtext: My question is, is this 13 per cent going to apply as the floor for 1957-58? I ask that question because under the policies followed by the present government everybody knows that the revenues of the government in 1958-59 are bound to decline.

maintopic: DOMINION-PROVINCIAL RELATIONS MEASURE TO PROVIDE FINANCIAL ASSISTANCE TO ATLANTIC PROVINCES, ETC.

At the beginning of my remarks I said the Minister of Finance had misled the provincial governments and the country as a whole on Saturday last. Well, I really do not blame the Minister of Finance. maintopic: DOMINION-PROVINCIAL RELATIONS MEASURE TO PROVIDE FINANCIAL ASSISTANCE TO ATLANTIC PROVINCES, ETC.

maintopic: DOMINION-PROVINCIAL RELATIONS MEASURE TO PROVIDE FINANCIAL ASSISTANCE TO ATLANTIC PROVINCES, ETC.
speechtext: Nonsense.

maintopic: DOMINION-PROVINCIAL RELATIONS MEASURE TO PROVIDE FINANCIAL ASSISTANCE TO ATLANTIC PROVINCES, ETC.

[Mr. Lesage.1

Mr. Chairman, I do however derive some sort of satisfaction out of this government's proposal when I think of the statements made in this house by Conservative members from Quebec in July, 1956, when Mr. Harris submitted his resolution for the implementation of the fiscal agreements we have today, and of the promises made by the Conservatives during the 1957 election campaign. These gentlemen, including the Solicitor General, could not find words strong enough to denounce as a centralizing measure the equalization formula developed by the Liberal government, although today they endorse and ratify this very formula. As witness page 5989 of the official record, on July 16, 1956 the Solicitor General made in this house the following statement:
... it must have . . .
He was referring to the government of the province of Quebec,
... it must have the power to legislate on all matters pertaining to education within the province. The power to legislate cannot operate soundly without the power to tax for the same ends, and that power cannot operate soundly if the province is at the mercy of the central government's subsidies.
The Solicitor General was outspokenly opposing the payment of subsidies to the provinces under the equalization formula then being considered by the house. Today, he is of one mind with a government which recognizes its inability to find a better solution than that of the right hon. member for Quebec East (Mr. St. Laurent), which was then applied by Mr. Harris, then minister of finance.

Oh! oh!
If, as early as October 18, 1957, the Solicitor General had, with the help of his colleagues from the cabinet, devised some other formula which was likely to prove satisfactory to all provinces, as well as to himself, why was it not suggested to the provinces last November? The Right Hon. Prime Minister (Mr. Diefenbaker) did not say a word about it; on the contrary, he embarked upon three diversionary proposals.
Why dilly-dally? Why not act right now? Why should a solution be imposed to the provinces by telegram? Was it not the Solicitor General who, on July 16, 1956, said in the house, as reported on page 6029 of Hansard:
In fact, the resolution moved by the hon. Minister of Finance (Mr. Harris) and upon which we are called upon to pass judgment is not the result of a conference between the federal government and the provinces; not at all. We are not being asked to ratify an agreement between the dominion government and the provinces, an agreement reached following long negotiations where every party concerned had previously examined the proposals made. On the contrary, once again the federal government acted in a centralizing and unilateral way. It called the provinces together, read out its proposal . . .
And that, Mr. Chairman, is more than was done by the present government.
. . . and asked them what they thought about it, made a few minor changes here and there and said: "Do as you wish, this is as far as we can go".
What a joke, Mr. Chairman, at a time when the present government is dictating its views to the provinces by means of unappealable telegrams. Those telegrams went out last Friday whereas the resolution was in Saturday's Votes and Proceedings and by yesterday we were being asked to consider

Dominion-Provincial Relations it so as to stop the provinces from making their reaction known. Is not this a "centralizing and unilateral procedure", if I may borrow the Solicitor General's own phrase?
How can the Solicitor General hope to be taken seriously in his province and in the country as a whole-

I say again, Mr. Chairman, we are dealing with a turnabout government, a government of electoral expedients and of ill-applied poultices. The Canadian people are well aware of the fact and the day will not come too soon when it will enjoy the satisfaction of again returning a sound, honest and Liberal administration.

maintopic: DOMINION-PROVINCIAL RELATIONS MEASURE TO PROVIDE FINANCIAL ASSISTANCE TO ATLANTIC PROVINCES, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, my main purpose in rising at this time is to ask the minister who is piloting this resolution through the committee to answer some questions which have not yet been answered.
One of the matters brought out yesterday was that the position of the Conservative party in the past has been that there should be a reallocation of the taxing powers of the federal government and the provincial governments, so that each would have its sphere of taxation and would be able to look after its own obligations under the constitution without having to resort to the federal government.
I understood, and I think the people of Canada understood, that this was the basic approach of the members of the present government when in opposition, the basic approach of their attack upon the various federal-provincial agreements that had been negotiated with the provinces by the Liberal government. I think the Minister of Finance should definitely answer this question when he deals with the matter.
When the members of the present government, the Progressive Conservatives, are following exactly the formula found in the present tax agreements, are increasing the amount of personal income tax payable to the provinces from 10 per cent to 13 per cent, and are not departing from the principle of equalization in any way at all, I ask them whether they have now decided that they cannot go any farther with the policy about which they made such a great play over the

last three or four years. In other words, have they definitely abandoned the policy with respect to which they made such an appeal over the last three or four years?
I tried to draw some conclusion from the remarks of the Minister of Finance with respect to this matter, and the only conclusion I could draw was that they have abandoned this policy, that they now propose to proceed under the policy which they criticized so bitterly when they were in opposition. If they have not abandoned their basic policy of giving the provinces some reallocation of taxation rights, what I do not understand is why they did not place some suggestion of their own policy before the conference last November.
One cannot help but wonder if they did not seize on the formula of saying they were not going to dictate anything, they were going to listen to what the provinces had to say, in order to avoid bringing any proposals of their own before that conference. In other words, if they had found a solution to the problem, as they claimed to have done when they were appealing to the people, why did they not at least lay it before the conference for consideration by the provinces and by the people of Canada?
It seems to me, Mr. Chairman, that the only inference one can draw is that they now have no policy of their own and they do not know anything they can suggest to replace the policy which they criticized when in opposition.

maintopic: DOMINION-PROVINCIAL RELATIONS MEASURE TO PROVIDE FINANCIAL ASSISTANCE TO ATLANTIC PROVINCES, ETC.
speechtext: And which they do not understand themselves even now.

maintopic: DOMINION-PROVINCIAL RELATIONS MEASURE TO PROVIDE FINANCIAL ASSISTANCE TO ATLANTIC PROVINCES, ETC.
speechtext:
It has been suggested that they do not understand it themselves. In any event they should understand the alternative policy which they professed to be ready to bring forward. Surely it would not have been any infringement on the rights of the provinces to have done so. Indeed, the provinces must have been waiting with the expectation that when at the November conference they brought forward their suggestions, they would hear the great new proposals of the Progressive Conservative party, the party that was going to respect the rights of the provinces, the party that was going to respect their autonomy, the party that was going to solve this whole question so that all provinces would be able to exercise their constitutional obligations based upon the powers the Progressive Conservatives were going to give them.
Where are these proposals? It looks to me, Mr. Chairman, as if the Progressive Conservative party is manoeuvring around to

avoid bringing forward these proposals if they have them. I doubt very much if they have them, but if they do have them then I suggest they are afraid to bring them forward. They hope somehow or other to manoeuvre the political situation in this country in such a way that they can get a verdict of the people without disclosing what they have in mind in this regard. In fairness to the people of the country I suggest that before the government ever thinks of dissolving the house and asking for a verdict of the people they should tell the people just what they really have in mind. They avoided doing so by calling this conference into session last November for the short time it sat, making no proposals themselves and now bringing forward a set of proposals which have all the earmarks of a preelection offer, without in any way bringing forward the great proposals which they were supposed to have for the provinces.
I do suggest that if they have the respect for parliament and the people of the country they claim to have they should, instead of manoeuvring around as they are doing and trying to avoid disclosing what they have in mind, give the people of the country the information they are entitled to have as to what a Tory government would do if it had an overall majority and so the power to act which it is constantly saying it would like to have. If they intend to depart from these principles which are a real protection to the maritime and prairie provinces, the weaker provinces financially, then before the people are asked to vote the government should tell them what they intend to do instead of hiding their policy under these makeshift arrangements.
I suggest to the Minister of Finance and the Prime Minister that if they go to the people without disclosing what they intend to do with regard to this matter that is so important to us, then the people of western Canada and the Atlantic provinces will be entitled to draw their own conclusions as to what they intend to do. Therefore I suggest to the Minister of Finance that the government should bring forward what it has in mind as other than an interim solution to the problem. If they intend to ask for the support of the people, let them say what they have in mind as their own policy.
There is another point on which I should like to ask the minister to give us some information. Why was such a sudden decision made? When the conference met last fall the representatives of the provincial governments were led to believe that another conference would be held early this year. Such a conference has not been held on the
Dominion-Provincial Relations perfectly flimsy excuse that it could not be held while parliament was in session, an excuse which nobody accepts as a sound reason. There was nothing to prevent the government shortening the hours of sitting of the house after Christmas to the same length as when the conference met in November, and having just the same amount of time to deal with these matters as they had in November.
As a matter of fact, they have had many opportunities. When our convention was being held it was suggested by members of the opposition parties that the house sittings be lightened so those matters could be attended to. Why did the government not arrange for the conference to meet again at that time? As a matter of fact, quite clearly they did not want another conference before the event with which they are always preoccupying themselves instead of dealing with the great problems facing the country, twice as many unemployed as we have ever had since we started to keep figures, great problems of trade, and all the rest of our problems.
No; they are concerned about getting themselves in a position where they think they may be able to snatch a verdict from the people before they disclose their policies. I suggest, Mr. Chairman, that before the people of the country place any further confidence in the members of the present government they will want to know where the government stands on these various problems. Their decision in this matter was a sudden decision-and everything shows that it was-so sudden that the government itself did not take the time to have its expert advisers work out exactly what would be coming to each province under that decision. If they had given their advisers a matter of 24 hours notice we would not have the mistakes that were admitted by the Minister of Finance. He admits that mistakes were made in figuring out the effect of the proposal, that certain clauses of the act were overlooked. He cannot make the people of the country or the members of this house believe that they would have been overlooked by the civil servants who are used to dealing with these matters.
In other words, Mr. Chairman, this is a decision taken for political purposes and announced throughout the country on the spur of the moment. This is the sort of government we have been getting, no considered judgment, no decisions other than looking to the time when a sudden dissolution of parliament can be brought about and an attempt made to snatch some sort of decision from the people without giving them the exact facts.

Dominion-Provincial Relations
I suggest that there is another reason. The minister had to admit that in making this announcement he had not taken into account important matters having to do with the decision he had just made. At page 3875 of Hansard for January 27, 1958, he said:
The figures given on Saturday morning have to be read in the light of the stabilization principle, and the figures that were put on the record this afternoon represent the final figures and take account of all the elements in the tax-sharing arrangement.
In other words, when the minister made the announcement to parliament, and when he advised the premiers as to what the government was offering, he did not take into account all the elements that were involved, according to his own admission. Does that not give an indication to the house of the haste with which they were trying to get this proposal before the people?
There is another thing. If there was one thing that the government opposite, when in opposition, found fault with it was this business of handing out propositions to the provinces without consulting them. Could there be any worse example of that attitude than what has just taken place? They called the provinces together, the provinces submitted their wishes, and according to Premier Campbell there was agreement on certain things upon the condition that another conference would be held which would deal with these matters. Then the provinces received a telegram indicating that the government was going to do certain things. I doubt very much if the government would have taken that high-handed action if they did not have some definite political advantage in mind, because by so doing they have broken with the very basis upon which they attacked the previous government.
We were told by the Minister of Finance that this decision was based upon agreement with all the provinces. In that regard I believe some attention should be paid to the attitude of the premier of Manitoba, and I should like to read from the premier's letter to the Prime Minister. He said, as reported at page 3227 of Hansard for January 11, 1958:
My colleagues and I feel that it is advisable now to restate Manitoba's position on one question which, to our surprise, took precedence over even the most basic matters with which we had hoped to deal.
I refer to the financial adjustments for the Atlantic provinces that were proposed by the federal government. At the conference itself Manitoba's position was stated as well as it could be on such short notice. You will recall that it was at federal insistence that the conference found itself having to deal with two or three specific matters, including the so-called Atlantic provinces adjustment, before the meeting broke up, while it appeared to the Manitoba representatives that

you and your ministers were unwilling, or unable, to deal with the broader question of the general financial arrangements between the federal and provincial governments.
Here was a conference called to deal with these general questions, and the premier of Manitoba said the federal government was either unable or unwilling to deal with them. Then he went on:
In any event, because of the insistence by you and your colleagues in the last hours of our two-day meeting that this specific matter had to be dealt with at that particular moment, we had no time to prepare a full and studied statement of Manitoba's position in this connection.
In other words this subject was sprung on the conference, and the federal government insisted that it be dealt with without giving the provinces an opportunity to make representations on the matter. Then Premier Campbell said this:
Our proposal will readily be seen to mean an extra $40 million for the Atlantic provinces. This extra assistance to that part of our nation would, under our plan, be available through a formula which would apply equally to all sections of Canada and which would mean that all Canadian citizens would be treated equally by our main tax-sharing arrangements.
Premier Campbell went on to point out:
We also emphasized the point that adverse weather conditions or other unfavourable circumstances might place one or all of the prairie provinces in the same position and consequently that the policy should not be termed an Atlantic adjustment but one applicable to any province of Canada where the need is established.
Surely if there is one thing that should be accepted by the government of Canada it is that any principle that is applied to one province should be applied to all provinces. It was on that basis that the provinces agreed to something being done for a part of Canada which it was said needed help. The agreement was made on the basis that it should be understood and declared that that policy should apply to all of Canada.
There has been no such declaration. All we have heard from the Minister of Finance so far is that under present circumstances the principle would not apply to other provinces in Canada. We have not had an authoritative declaration that if circumstances did result in the income of the people of other parts of Canada being reduced the principle would apply to them as a matter of law.
This is a very important declaration by the premier of Manitoba. Certainly the Prime Minister knows that a poor crop could strike down the economy of the prairie provinces and place them in a position where their governments might very well be unable to carry out their constitutional obligations, and where they would need the

same sort of principle applied to them as is being applied to the Atlantic provinces.
Why is it that we cannot have an authoritative declaration that the principle will apply to all provinces, as requested by the premier of Manitoba? Why has the premier of Manitoba not been given a definite answer? This is a matter that should be explained when the Minister of Finance answers.
Then, too, the premier of Manitoba points out that it was stated to the conference that the cost of these Atlantic settlements, the provisions in regard to unemployment insurance, and the provisions in regard to paying the extra cost if tuberculosis patients and mental cases are included in the hospital insurance plan, would come out of the general federal-provincial program. In that regard I should like to read what Premier Campbell said in his letter and I think the minister should clear this up beyond any doubt. Premier Campbell said:
You and your ministers-
This is directed to the Prime Minister-
-also declared It to be your policy that if the provinces agreed to any of these three specific items the resulting costs would have to be subtracted from whatever amount might be available for the future general dominion-provincial fiscal rearrangements which will most directly benefit municipalities and provinces.
Is it true that what we are doing at this time, although allegedly on an interim basis, in regard to any of these matters is going to affect the ultimate amount that may be distributed under the general fiscal arrangements with the provinces? If that is so, then anything we do now is another dictate to the provinces, something upon which they have not been consulted, because they have never agreed to this proposition. Now then, Mr. Chairman-

It was generally agreed that the over-all economic position of the Atlantic provinces is now such as to justify some special grants in aid to the governments of those provinces from the federal government.

-without any question. Before the intervention of the Prime Minister I was dealing with three matters; let him also deal with these three matters. He was willing to deal with one. If they do decide that the tuberculosis and mental costs should be included under the hospital insurance scheme, is that going to be charged to the provinces? The Prime Minister dealt with one question, now let him deal with the others.
If there is a great deal of money spent in the policy of removing the threshold so far as assistance to the provinces in dealing with unemployed is concerned-and of course there will be a great deal of money spent in

Dominion-Provincial Relations that connection-is that going to come out of the money which ordinarily would go to help the provinces under these fiscal arrangements under decisions made at the dominion-provincial conferences? Premier Campbell said that was the stated policy of the government, and I say the government should be prepared to say whether that is true or whether they have changed their minds since the conference, because the people of this country are entitled to know what the situation is before they vote.
The next matter which I think the government should clear up without any delay and without any doubt is this. They say, "Pass this and we, if we are left in power, are some time later going to amend the Income Tax Act." This is in regard to those parts of Canada where there is double taxation; but they are avoiding taking a position on this matter with respect to what they are going to do. Why is it that they do not take the people into their confidence and say what they are going to do, instead of asking parliament to vote without knowing what is their true position?
I would therefore suggest that the people of Canada are entitled to an answer, and the Prime Minister was very ready to get up and answer me before. Let him answer this question. Have they abandoned their policy whereby they insisted that the right attitude in this matter was to reallocate the fields of taxation as between the federal government and the provinces? Have they abandoned that policy? Let him answer that, and let him also answer why there was the sudden decision to put out this proposal before the civil servants had a chance to even calculate what it would mean to each province. Why that sudden decision? Did they make the sudden decision having in mind the possible dissolution of this parliament in an attempt to snatch a decision from the people?

speechtext: Oh, oh.

maintopic: DOMINION-PROVINCIAL RELATIONS MEASURE TO PROVIDE FINANCIAL ASSISTANCE TO ATLANTIC PROVINCES, ETC.
speechtext:
Hon. members can laugh, but that does not answer me. Let him also answer, in addition to that question, whether he is prepared to extend the same rights to all the provinces that he is extending in this particular instance to the Atlantic provinces and of which he is making so much. As Premier Campbell said, we of the west are glad to see the weaker provinces assisted properly as is being done in this matter, but we want to know if this policy is going to apply to all provinces. In other words, will this great Liberal policy which has given the foundation upon which the provinces can exercise their constitutional obligations, be carried forward in its entirety to all parts

of Canada, or will an attempt be made to make an election bribe out of it for one part of Canada?
The next thing I would like to raise is that I think the Prime Minister should say whether these things that were said in regard to mental and tuberculosis costs and in regard to unemployment assistance costs are going to have to come out of the amount of money the provinces might get under this policy of general fiscal arrangements.
Let the Prime Minister deal with these matters, but above all let him tell us as to the basis upon which this appeal was made to the people of Canada, namely that the Liberal party were centralizing because they were raising taxes and turning money over to the provinces, which was necessary in order for them to carry out their constitutional obligations and that there should be a reallocation of taxing powers so that each province should levy its own taxes and run its own affairs. Has this policy now been abandoned? Let him tell the pleople of Canada as to that.

maintopic: DOMINION-PROVINCIAL RELATIONS MEASURE TO PROVIDE FINANCIAL ASSISTANCE TO ATLANTIC PROVINCES, ETC.
speechtext:
I
would remind the ministry in the presence of the Minister of Finance and the Prime Minister that the province of British Columbia sometimes, and this has certainly been the case in the past, feels that it is inclined to be forgotten; and remind them that there is indeed a province on the other side of the mountains. It has already been mentioned that British Columbia awoke on Saturday morning to expect a further $5| million, but on Monday morning that amount had been cut to $2.8 million; and it has been suggested that cut could be described as the "most unkindest cut of all" which occurred over this week end.
The minister has changed the formula, which is an extremely complicated one in a way, unfortunately, which favours the provinces of Ontario and Quebec unduly and which gives too little consideration to the province of British Columbia. The net advantage to the province of British Columbia has been described as $2.8 million or almost $3 million, while in the case of the province of Ontario the net advantage is going to be $22 million. The population of the province of Ontario is only four times that of the province of British Columbia, yet the expected increase under this change in formula will be about eight times our increase. In other words, in Ontario, they are receiving twice as favourable consideration under the new formula as under the old formula.
In the case of the province of Quebec, which is now going to receive an additional

Dominion-Provincial Relations
$19 million, this is approximately six times the benefit being received by the province of British Columbia, yet the population of Quebec is only three times that of my own province. So once again approximately double the consideration is being given to Quebec that is being given to British Columbia.
I therefore suggest that the minister should give consideration to this matter, and I furthermore suggest that he is treating my province in this necessary readjustment as somewhat the neglected child of confederation. As we are still at the resolution stage I suggest it is not too late for him to revise his proposals in order to do away with this inequity to my own province. I am not comparing my province with, say, the prairie provinces or the Atlantic regions, because they do have special problems of their own. But it is true to say that British Columbia, as an industrial province, is more comparable with Quebec and Ontario and, as they are comparable, I say that the more favoured treatment being given to the two central provinces is unfair and warrants reconsideration by the Minister of Finance.

maintopic: DOMINION-PROVINCIAL RELATIONS MEASURE TO PROVIDE FINANCIAL ASSISTANCE TO ATLANTIC PROVINCES, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, the
measure to provide financial assistance to the Atlantic provinces by authorizing the paying out of the consolidated revenue fund for each of the four years commencing on the 1st day of April of this year of an annual grant of $7$ million to each of the provinces of New Brunswick, Nova Scotia and Newfoundland, and an annual grant of $2J million to the province of Prince Edward Island, and also to raise from 10 per cent to 13 per cent the rate paid to the provinces under the Federal-Provincial Tax-Sharing Arrangements Act, is welcomed, I am sure, by all members of this house.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: DOMINION-PROVINCIAL RELATIONS MEASURE TO PROVIDE FINANCIAL ASSISTANCE TO ATLANTIC PROVINCES, ETC.
speechtext: You would not think so to listen to the last three speakers.

maintopic: DOMINION-PROVINCIAL RELATIONS MEASURE TO PROVIDE FINANCIAL ASSISTANCE TO ATLANTIC PROVINCES, ETC.
speechtext:
My remarks, Mr. Chairman, will deal chiefly with the $7J million in equalization grants which will be paid to the province of New Brunswick. I realize it is not possible for this government to designate a set portion of this equalization grant to be paid directly to the municipalities. Nevertheless I would like to see a suggestion from this government to the provincial government that special consideration be given by the provinces to safeguard the rights of the municipalities.
The distribution of the amount under the federal-provincial tax-sharing agreements by the province of New Brunswick to its municipalities has been a bone of contention over the years, in that the municipalities have claimed they have never received their
inherent and rightful share despite all the efforts made for an equitable distribution.
From 1952 until the present time federal grants in lieu of taxation rose from approximately $8 million to $24 million, an increase to three times the 1952 amount. The municipalities received a very small share of the increased grants, despite the fact that school costs and other costs are mounting at an alarming rate, with the result that rural taxpayers in most counties in New Brunswick are finding it extremely difficult to pay municipal taxes, which are steadily rising despite all the efforts of municipal councils to keep down costs.
In the year 1951-52 the province of New Brunswick received $11,274,523 in direct payments from the federal treasury under the province's share of income tax from certain corporations and from statutory subsidies. Over the years tax rental agreement payments substantially increased with the expanding economy, and in the year 1955-56 the total amount paid in direct payments was $18,517,000.
The increase that would be received by the provinces for the fiscal year 1957-58 over the 1956-57 figure, as estimated by Mr. Harris, former minister of finance, on page 5889 of Hansard of July 16, 1956, was $114 million. This estimate showed New Brunswick as receiving $7,375,000 on yield of standard taxes and equalization payments of $14,705,-
000.	These amounts, with the statutory grant of $1,670,000, made a total of $23,759,000 estimated for New Brunswick for 1957-58. The amount tabled yesterday shows $23,490,000 paid in 1957-58.
Under the bill which will follow this resolution the province of New Brunswick will receive $7,500,000 from Atlantic adjustment grants and an interim payment based on the increase from 10 per cent to 13 per cent under the federal-provincial tax arrangements in the amount of $2,111,000, for a total of $9,611,000. This $9,611,000 together with the normal payments under the federal-provincial tax sharing agreement and the statutory subsidies will reach a total of over $30 million which will be received by New Brunswick for the fiscal year 1958-59.
When the minister closes this debate I should like him to inform me if the figure of $30 million can be considered a fairly approximate one. It is realized that it is not possible to forecast a definite figure until the federal-provincial conference on fiscal matters concludes its deliberations later this year. In the minister's statement to the house on Saturday last, he said:
All provincial treasurers are preparing budgets for the fiscal year commencing April 1 and require

Dominion-Provincial Relations
to know immediately what, if any, additional fiscal payments they may expect to receive from the dominion government during the fiscal year.
It is interesting to note what action certain provinces announced they would take if increased grants were forthcoming. Premier Campbell of Manitoba stated he would turn over to the municipalities the full amount of any increases. The premier of Nova Scotia met with municipal officials of his province and discussed the sharing of increased grants with municipalities.
No known move has been made by the government of New Brunswick in this connection. The New Brunswick union of municipalities should demand an immediate conference on this important fiscal matter.
In regard to preparing provincial fiscal budgets and the statement of the Minister of Finance that it was important for provincial treasurers to know what they could expect, the same situation applies to municipal governments, and it is hoped that the province of New Brunswick will show the same attitude to the municipalities of that province.
The Minister of Finance, speaking on the resolution, said the Atlantic equalization grants and the interim amounts of increased tax sharing payments would assist public works projects which, in turn, would relieve unemployment. If the province of New Brunswick follows this suggestion the people of Northumberland-Miramichi are looking forward to the completion of the Renous-Plaster Rock road and a highway bridge across the Miramichi river at Chatham, public works projects long overdue. The people of New Brunswick expect fair treatment to be given the lower levels of government by the province in the sharing of the extra $10 million.

maintopic: DOMINION-PROVINCIAL RELATIONS MEASURE TO PROVIDE FINANCIAL ASSISTANCE TO ATLANTIC PROVINCES, ETC.
speechtext: May I point out to the hon. member that they would not have had the extra $10 million to share if his government had remained in power. He is very good at telling New Brunswick what to do, but there would have been no additional funds to hand out if it had not been for this government.

maintopic: DOMINION-PROVINCIAL RELATIONS MEASURE TO PROVIDE FINANCIAL ASSISTANCE TO ATLANTIC PROVINCES, ETC.
speechtext: However it came about they are going to get this $10 million, and I am doing my duty here in trying to see that this money is used to benefit the municipalities.

maintopic: DOMINION-PROVINCIAL RELATIONS MEASURE TO PROVIDE FINANCIAL ASSISTANCE TO ATLANTIC PROVINCES, ETC.
speechtext: May I inform the hon. member-

maintopic: DOMINION-PROVINCIAL RELATIONS MEASURE TO PROVIDE FINANCIAL ASSISTANCE TO ATLANTIC PROVINCES, ETC.
speechtext: Order.

maintopic: DOMINION-PROVINCIAL RELATIONS MEASURE TO PROVIDE FINANCIAL ASSISTANCE TO ATLANTIC PROVINCES, ETC.
speechtext: On a point of order, I believe that the Minister of Veterans Affairs will have all the opportunities he wishes to make statements on this question. He was not rising on a point of order, and he was not asking a question.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: DOMINION-PROVINCIAL RELATIONS MEASURE TO PROVIDE FINANCIAL ASSISTANCE TO ATLANTIC PROVINCES, ETC.
speechtext: He was asking a question of the hon. member who had the floor.

maintopic: DOMINION-PROVINCIAL RELATIONS MEASURE TO PROVIDE FINANCIAL ASSISTANCE TO ATLANTIC PROVINCES, ETC.
speechtext: He was cluttering Hansard.

maintopic: DOMINION-PROVINCIAL RELATIONS MEASURE TO PROVIDE FINANCIAL ASSISTANCE TO ATLANTIC PROVINCES, ETC.
speechtext: The hon. member was reading his statement. I was just asking a question.

maintopic: DOMINION-PROVINCIAL RELATIONS MEASURE TO PROVIDE FINANCIAL ASSISTANCE TO ATLANTIC PROVINCES, ETC.
speechtext: An unnecessary remark.

maintopic: DOMINION-PROVINCIAL RELATIONS MEASURE TO PROVIDE FINANCIAL ASSISTANCE TO ATLANTIC PROVINCES, ETC.
speechtext:
I felt that it was a fair observation by the Minister of Veterans Affairs if he wished to raise that point, and I personally do not have any objection to his raising it. But, I repeat, I feel I owe a duty to the municipality of Northumberland and to the province of New Brunswick, and I must point out that we expect fair treatment in this regard.
This resolution has my wholehearted support, and I trust that the government of the province of New Brunswick will carry out the spirit of this resolution and in turn make equalization payments to the municipalities, towns and cities. The citizens of New Brunswick are entitled to an early announcement as to how the New Brunswick government plans to expend this money. The municipalities want to know this now because it has a very important bearing on their annual budgets and tax structures. Most of the municipalities of New Brunswick will convene their annual sessions within the next two or three weeks. Some of them, in fact, are meeting this week.
As I indicated, Mr. Chairman, I will be pleased to support the passage of this resolution and the bill based thereon.

maintopic: DOMINION-PROVINCIAL RELATIONS MEASURE TO PROVIDE FINANCIAL ASSISTANCE TO ATLANTIC PROVINCES, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I have listened with interest to this debate. I was very much interested in the remarks made by my hon. friend from Northumberland-Miramichi who has just resumed his seat, though apparently some of the remarks he made did not meet with approval of other members from our province.
There is one thing I wish to deal with at this time, and that is the opening remarks of the Minister of Finance in introducing this resolution. I quote his own words, as reported at page 3847 of Hansard of yesterday's date:
Mr. Chairman, to the present resolution and to the bill which it is hoped will follow upon the passage of the resolution, the government attaches very great importance, for it looks upon this measure as one that will bring aid to the provinces and municipalities of this country, and effective aid also in meeting the problem of unemployment.
To my knowledge, Mr. Chairman, this is the first time in the history of the federal government's dealings with the provinces when assistance has been earmarked before it left the capital city. I know of no other occasion in my experience here when a

federal government has ever told the provinces for what purposes such assistance should be used, and I may add that I was here in 1945 when the premiers of the provinces were called together in conference to deal with the matter of federal-provincial tax rental agreements. This is the first case of its kind. We Liberals have always been able to boast that when these moneys were provided to the provinces they were provided with no strings attached, and were to be used for any purpose the provinces wished.
I will say before I am interrupted that every hon. member from the maritimes certainly welcomes this assistance to the maritime provinces. There can be no question about that. This represents, of course, a simple continuation of a time tested, good Liberal policy. It is nothing more or less than a continuation of good Liberal policy.

maintopic: DOMINION-PROVINCIAL RELATIONS MEASURE TO PROVIDE FINANCIAL ASSISTANCE TO ATLANTIC PROVINCES, ETC.
speechtext: They get the money now, though; that is the difference.

maintopic: DOMINION-PROVINCIAL RELATIONS MEASURE TO PROVIDE FINANCIAL ASSISTANCE TO ATLANTIC PROVINCES, ETC.
speechtext: By going into deficit, yes.

maintopic: DOMINION-PROVINCIAL RELATIONS MEASURE TO PROVIDE FINANCIAL ASSISTANCE TO ATLANTIC PROVINCES, ETC.
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, I can well remember when my hon. friend who just interrupted sat on this side of the house and condemned the federal-provincial tax rental arrangements on every occasion when they were brought into this house. I can go back to the leaders under whom he has sat in this house, and every one of those hon. gentlemen including his present leader condemned the federal-provincial tax rental agreements.

maintopic: DOMINION-PROVINCIAL RELATIONS MEASURE TO PROVIDE FINANCIAL ASSISTANCE TO ATLANTIC PROVINCES, ETC.
speechtext: Quote one instance for me when I condemned them.

maintopic: DOMINION-PROVINCIAL RELATIONS MEASURE TO PROVIDE FINANCIAL ASSISTANCE TO ATLANTIC PROVINCES, ETC.
speechtext: I was sitting as an observer in the Senate on the occasion when one of the leaders before the one under whom you sit now put his portfolio under his arm and walked out and scuttled that conference. He scuttled it and so did Maurice Duplessis, who is now premier of the province of Quebec.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: DOMINION-PROVINCIAL RELATIONS MEASURE TO PROVIDE FINANCIAL ASSISTANCE TO ATLANTIC PROVINCES, ETC.
speechtext: That is utterly untrue.

maintopic: DOMINION-PROVINCIAL RELATIONS MEASURE TO PROVIDE FINANCIAL ASSISTANCE TO ATLANTIC PROVINCES, ETC.
speechtext: That is not untrue. I was there at the time and I am only telling about an event I saw with my own eyes. The tax rental agreements had been condemned by every leader of the Tory party for years.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: DOMINION-PROVINCIAL RELATIONS MEASURE TO PROVIDE FINANCIAL ASSISTANCE TO ATLANTIC PROVINCES, ETC.
speechtext: Mr. King adjourned the conference sine die, and that was the end of it.

maintopic: DOMINION-PROVINCIAL RELATIONS MEASURE TO PROVIDE FINANCIAL ASSISTANCE TO ATLANTIC PROVINCES, ETC.
speechtext:
If my friend the Minister of Finance will just contain himself I will go back and refresh his memory and give him some of the background of these conferences. I did not interrupt the hon. gentleman when he was speaking. His memory may be as poor as it was when he
Dominion-Provincial Relations drafted this proposal last Saturday, because he made a bad mistake somewhere, which suggests to me that despite his ability his memory may not be as good as mine.
On every occasion since I have been here when these tax rental agreements came up for renewal those who now sit on the government side of the house sat on the opposition benches and condemned them from every angle they could. However, since the Minister of Finance is interrupting me I want to take this opportunity of pointing out to him the great difference between sitting on the government side of the house and sitting in the opposition. I propose to refer to the words used by the Minister of Finance on July 23, 1956, as recorded at page 6296 of Hansard of that date. At that time the minister, who was then the private hon. member for Eglinton, said:
There is no use, as far as Her Majesty's loyal opposition is concerned, asking us to approve a form of dominion-provincial fiscal arrangement which has not received the approval of a single provincial government.
These are the minister's own words.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: DOMINION-PROVINCIAL RELATIONS MEASURE TO PROVIDE FINANCIAL ASSISTANCE TO ATLANTIC PROVINCES, ETC.
speechtext: And very sound, too.

maintopic: DOMINION-PROVINCIAL RELATIONS MEASURE TO PROVIDE FINANCIAL ASSISTANCE TO ATLANTIC PROVINCES, ETC.
speechtext:
I continue:
If there could be, on the part of the federal government, a change of attitude, and after that change in attitude they will call a new conference, then fruitful results I am certain could be achieved. It would necessitate a fall session of parliament. We would be quite happy to see a fall session in order to achieve this praiseworthy object.
There was a man who was sitting in opposition as a private hon. member. We had been in session for nearly eight months, but he was prepared to come back for a special session of parliament in order to bring together the provincial governments to discuss this question. But today, when we have been sitting here for only three or four months, the same hon. member who now occupies the portfolio of Minister of Finance could not find time to call in the provinces for a discussion. It was the first time in the history of this country that we have had legislation by telegram.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: DOMINION-PROVINCIAL RELATIONS MEASURE TO PROVIDE FINANCIAL ASSISTANCE TO ATLANTIC PROVINCES, ETC.
speechtext: Oh, how absurd!

maintopic: DOMINION-PROVINCIAL RELATIONS MEASURE TO PROVIDE FINANCIAL ASSISTANCE TO ATLANTIC PROVINCES, ETC.
speechtext: What about budget by radio?

maintopic: DOMINION-PROVINCIAL RELATIONS MEASURE TO PROVIDE FINANCIAL ASSISTANCE TO ATLANTIC PROVINCES, ETC.
speechtext:
I said "telegram". I did not say "radio" and I did not say "out at an airport" either. I said "by telegram", and that is exactly what has taken place. How the attitude can change. It was of such great importance in 1956 that the Minister of Finance was prepared to come back for a special fall session of parliament in order to call in the provincial

Dominion-Provincial Relations premiers for a discussion of the proposal, but today we have legislation by telegram.
I would like to read for the benefit of my hon. friend the Minister of Veterans Affairs the remarks made by Hon. Hugh John Flemming, premier of our province, when he came to Ottawa in 1956 to attend the federal-provincial conference held in that year, by way of illustrating to my friend the different atmosphere that prevailed in 1956 from that which the provincial premiers found prevailing as a result of the attitude of the present government. Mr. Flemming said:
We are thankful that the situation as we meet today is in decided contrast to the troubled times which formed the sombre backgrounds of other conferences. Today, we gather during a period of unprecedented economic expansion and at a time, furthermore, when international tensions are less than for a number of years. No doubt many unforeseen dangers lie ahead, and grave political problems underlie the appearance of tranquility. Nevertheless, I would submit that here and now, we who are gathered in this room, have been granted a magnificent opportunity to achieve long sought national objectives, and it is in such a spirit that our New Brunswick delegation has come to Ottawa.

maintopic: DOMINION-PROVINCIAL RELATIONS MEASURE TO PROVIDE FINANCIAL ASSISTANCE TO ATLANTIC PROVINCES, ETC.
speechtext: Mr. Flemming was referring to the war.

maintopic: DOMINION-PROVINCIAL RELATIONS MEASURE TO PROVIDE FINANCIAL ASSISTANCE TO ATLANTIC PROVINCES, ETC.
speechtext: Would you like to have the date on which these remarks were made? I was referring to the verbatim report of the proceedings of the federal-provincial conference held on Monday, October 3, 1955, some ten years after the war; and I would point out to my hon. friend that Hon. Hugh John Flemming was not premier of New Brunswick during the war. Your memory seems to be slipping since you have become Minister of Veterans Affairs.

maintopic: DOMINION-PROVINCIAL RELATIONS MEASURE TO PROVIDE FINANCIAL ASSISTANCE TO ATLANTIC PROVINCES, ETC.
speechtext: Not a bit.

maintopic: DOMINION-PROVINCIAL RELATIONS MEASURE TO PROVIDE FINANCIAL ASSISTANCE TO ATLANTIC PROVINCES, ETC.
speechtext:
I suspect there is something in that. I would like to quote another paragraph from Mr. Flemming's remarks, if I may:
We should continue to profit by the experience of the years in which the tax rental agreements have been operative. Undoubtedly, much has been learned of their benefit both from a provincial standpoint and from a federal point of view. The element of fiscal control should not be lightly dropped. So to summarize briefly we favour continuation of tax rental agreements with renewal clause for protection of the province.
Until this session of parliament I have never heard either my hon. friend the Minister of Veterans Affairs or my hon. friend the Minister of Finance pay a compliment to the federal-provincial tax rental agreements. When Hon. J. B. McNair was premier of our province, and ever since, the premiers have known that it was only under the tax rental agreements that the maritimes could provide the services to the people they have provided.

They could not operate without this assistance, which was granted over the protests of Hon. George Drew and Hon. Leslie Frost, premier of Ontario, and Maurice Duplessis, the premier of Quebec.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: DOMINION-PROVINCIAL RELATIONS MEASURE TO PROVIDE FINANCIAL ASSISTANCE TO ATLANTIC PROVINCES, ETC.
speechtext: No, it was not.

maintopic: DOMINION-PROVINCIAL RELATIONS MEASURE TO PROVIDE FINANCIAL ASSISTANCE TO ATLANTIC PROVINCES, ETC.
speechtext: The Minister of Finance can sit there and tell me it is not true but I know it is true.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: DOMINION-PROVINCIAL RELATIONS MEASURE TO PROVIDE FINANCIAL ASSISTANCE TO ATLANTIC PROVINCES, ETC.
speechtext: And I say it is not true.

maintopic: DOMINION-PROVINCIAL RELATIONS MEASURE TO PROVIDE FINANCIAL ASSISTANCE TO ATLANTIC PROVINCES, ETC.
speechtext:
I know it is true. They were opposed to it. They said they did not feel they should share the revenues of their own provinces. This was stated publicly and otherwise. The Minister of Finance may sit in this house and blatantly deny it, but to no avail because I know it is true. That has been the attitude down through the years.
I mentioned at the outset that this is the first occasion in my memory when it has ever been suggested by a minister of finance in making an announcement of this sort for what purpose the assistance was to be used. When the minister introduced this resolution he pointed out very clearly that he was most hopeful that it would be helpful in meeting the problem of unemployment.
I believe there may have been a political motive in making that suggestion. However, I was pleased to learn that the Minister of Finance has at last acknowledged that a serious unemployment situation exists in the province of New Brunswick and throughout the nation because we have been told on other occasions that it was just propaganda that was being circulated by the Liberals to try to instil fear into the Canadian people that would be most harmful to the economy of the country. Now, however, the Minister of Finance has at last acknowledged that we have a grave unemployment situation.
I can assure him that the money could be used to great advantage in the province of New Brunswick for this purpose, because in my own county today and in other counties of which I have records we have the most serious unemployment we have had in 25 years. It is most serious. I do hope it may be used for that purpose because today workers, particularly married men with families who are seeking employment and are unable to find it, certainly will appreciate having something to do so they can provide for their families during the long winter months. I for one think it might be a very good suggestion, that it would be helpful in the unemployment situation.
In his remarks in introducing the legislation yesterday the Minister of Finance tried to give the impression to those who were not

acquainted with the circumstances surrounding this most important subject that this was the first time any assistance had ever been given to the maritime provinces, or to any other part of Canada, under this tax-sharing arrangement. I should like to point out to the minister that this improvement is approximately a 12 per cent increase. The total amount given to the provinces under the tax rental agreement was $631 million, previous to this supplementary payment which has been made. That $631 million was provided to the provinces of this country by a Liberal administration.
To that the present government has added $87 million. In other words 88 per cent of the moneys provided under the federal-provincial tax rental agreement has been provided by a Liberal government and, as I stated a while ago, that amount has been provided in the face of prolonged and bitter opposition by those who now form the government, who have argued from every point of view that this system was wrong and that some other kind of system must be found to take its place. It certainly came as a great surprise to those of us sitting on this side of the house to discover as well that the Minister of Finance was using the formula adopted by his predecessor, Hon. Walter Harris, in working out additional payments, though I must say that Mr. Harris was much more careful with the figures he used than the Minister of Finance was a few days ago in the formula which the Tory members had condemned completely and entirely when they sat in the opposition.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: DOMINION-PROVINCIAL RELATIONS MEASURE TO PROVIDE FINANCIAL ASSISTANCE TO ATLANTIC PROVINCES, ETC.
speechtext: Because it was inadequate.

maintopic: DOMINION-PROVINCIAL RELATIONS MEASURE TO PROVIDE FINANCIAL ASSISTANCE TO ATLANTIC PROVINCES, ETC.
speechtext:
Surely the great knowledge of the Minister of Finance and his colleagues could have been used to work out a more just and a less complicated plan. I would have thought his ever present pride would have made it impossible for the Minister of Finance to admit that he was using a formula which had been worked out by the former minister of finance.
I have heard the Minister of Finance refer to the unfortunate inheritance of Liberal ideas and principles. He has referred to that so often-

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: DOMINION-PROVINCIAL RELATIONS MEASURE TO PROVIDE FINANCIAL ASSISTANCE TO ATLANTIC PROVINCES, ETC.
speechtext: Not the ideas and the principles; it was just the mess they left on the doorstep.

maintopic: DOMINION-PROVINCIAL RELATIONS MEASURE TO PROVIDE FINANCIAL ASSISTANCE TO ATLANTIC PROVINCES, ETC.
speechtext:
May I tell him that they have served him and his government very well, not only on this occasion but on every other occasion in working out the changes which have taken place since last June 22, with the exception of the trading policies of this country which speak for themselves.
Dominion-Provincial Relations
I do regret that the provincial premiers were denied the privilege of meeting with the federal government before this take it or leave it proposition was made. I believe it would be completely out of order for the Minister of Finance to direct the provincial authorities as to the way in which he feels this money should be spent. So often in the past I have heard the Minister of Finance refer to the Liberal government as being dictatorial. Well, I can assure the minister that no more glaring example of a dictatorial attitude can be found anywhere than in this legislation by telegram, not calling the provincial premiers to the capital city and not giving them any opportunity of expressing their views in this regard. It was purely a snap proposition, something to which very little consideration was given.
I believe we must all agree that the way it was presented on Saturday would indicate that no great thought had been given to the matter. It was very obvious at that time that the press in most parts of the country in expressing their views felt that it looked as though it might be something that would be done just previous to the announcement of an election date.
Before I resume my seat I should like to put on record an editorial which appeared in the Ottawa Citizen yesterday.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: DOMINION-PROVINCIAL RELATIONS MEASURE TO PROVIDE FINANCIAL ASSISTANCE TO ATLANTIC PROVINCES, ETC.
speechtext: That is out of order. You cannot put on the record an editorial pertaining to a current debate in parliament.

maintopic: DOMINION-PROVINCIAL RELATIONS MEASURE TO PROVIDE FINANCIAL ASSISTANCE TO ATLANTIC PROVINCES, ETC.
speechtext: What is that?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: DOMINION-PROVINCIAL RELATIONS MEASURE TO PROVIDE FINANCIAL ASSISTANCE TO ATLANTIC PROVINCES, ETC.
speechtext: The hon. member cannot read editorials on what is current in parliament.

maintopic: DOMINION-PROVINCIAL RELATIONS MEASURE TO PROVIDE FINANCIAL ASSISTANCE TO ATLANTIC PROVINCES, ETC.
speechtext: Is the Minister of Finance the chairman of the committee at this time?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: DOMINION-PROVINCIAL RELATIONS MEASURE TO PROVIDE FINANCIAL ASSISTANCE TO ATLANTIC PROVINCES, ETC.
speechtext: You ought to know the rules by now.

maintopic: DOMINION-PROVINCIAL RELATIONS MEASURE TO PROVIDE FINANCIAL ASSISTANCE TO ATLANTIC PROVINCES, ETC.
speechtext: The Minister of Finance is trying to direct the Chair.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: DOMINION-PROVINCIAL RELATIONS MEASURE TO PROVIDE FINANCIAL ASSISTANCE TO ATLANTIC PROVINCES, ETC.
speechtext: You ought to know the rules by now.

maintopic: DOMINION-PROVINCIAL RELATIONS MEASURE TO PROVIDE FINANCIAL ASSISTANCE TO ATLANTIC PROVINCES, ETC.
speechtext: I should say this, Mr. Chairman. The Minister of Finance is muttering to himself and he has suggested that I should know the rules, but I want to say this since he has made that assertion. In my experience here in 12 or 13 years no one has broken the rules of this house to the same extent as the minister who sits across from me. In my experience no one has made any sillier interjections than has the Minister of Finance.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: DOMINION-PROVINCIAL RELATIONS MEASURE TO PROVIDE FINANCIAL ASSISTANCE TO ATLANTIC PROVINCES, ETC.
speechtext:
The rule is being broken by you today.

Dominion-Provincial Relations

maintopic: DOMINION-PROVINCIAL RELATIONS MEASURE TO PROVIDE FINANCIAL ASSISTANCE TO ATLANTIC PROVINCES, ETC.
