It is a pleasure for me to state very frankly, Mr. Speaker, that this bill is a very long overdue measure which should have been introduced in this house a good many years ago.
I would like to take very briefly the position in one industry, the paper industry, because it is with that industry that I am most concerned within my own riding. The lack of a minimum wage law affects many thousands of people in my riding in a very adverse way. What happens with these pulp mills, of course, is that where the unions are strong and where employees are in unions they are in a position to obtain fair minimum wages, at least generally speaking. However, where our people are being exploited is where they are engaged in secondary industries, and the difficulty is that it is almost impossible to unionize and get together.
As the price of paper goes up, for instance, I have found in my riding that the prices the farmers receive for their pulpwood goes down and down, and it might be reasonably ascertained that the person who is being punished is the fellow who is not in a position to appeal to a union to press for reasonable wages. For 22 years the former government sat by indifferently and lazily, neglecting to introduce a fair minimum wage act. This has been a growing problem in this country for a good many years, and I can well remember former government members going down to my riding during election time and promising these minimum wage acts, but this is the first time I have had a chance to speak on this

subject. I congratulate the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre for bringing this bill before the house at this time.
Right at this time in my own riding the C.N.R., for instance, is paying 70 cents an hour for snow shovellers while the C.P.R., right across on the next track, is paying something like $1.15 or $1.20 an hour. We find all through the story that it is precisely those men who are most in need of this type of protection who are expected to work for wages which are far below what might be considered necessary in order to maintain a reasonable standard of living.
I must also congratulate the government of the province of New Brunswick which, since 1952, has introduced a minimum wage act of its own. This has gone a long way toward alleviating the injustices which were perpetrated against employees in my province. Of course, so far as I can find out Liberal policies have always been against minimum wages, and it is most unfortunate that we have had to wait until this late in the day to have occasion to approve this measure.
I wish to make just one more point; that it will be found as the result of a minimum of inquiry that this bill will do no more than provide the merest form of justice to employees. The bill possibly does not go far enough, but it would be a great step forward and I sincerely urge the acceptance of this bill by the house.

In principle, Mr. Speaker, I am in agreement with the bill now put forward by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre. It has long been recognized and believed that a minimum wage for employees in general is required. Of course we have to accept the fact in this particular instance that the bill relates only to federal employees, and those people in allied services. As has been said, in this house we cannot attempt to legislate an over-all minimum wage act, but certainly in a situation of this kind the government of Canada should take the lead and so far as it is within the legislative authority of the parliament of Canada such a minimum wage act should be brought in.
Having said these few words on the general principle of the bill, I would like to discuss in detail some of the principles as they are found in individual clauses. The first clause to which I wish to refer is clause 3 of the bill, which is the application of the bill to employees. This seems to be the customary type of clause which has been put in other acts, as the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre has pointed out. I find the same provision and the same application in other bills which have been put forward

by the hon. member, and also in a bill put forward by the Minister of Labour in relation to the same matter.
The other section to which I should like to refer is clause 5. Clause 5 is a principle which I think was well placed in this particular bill. It does not seem at first glance that it is necessarily a part of a minimum wage bill. It merely requires an employer to provide any necessary special wearing apparel, equipment and so forth to an employee without any deduction being made in this respect. However, on more careful examination it can be seen that there might be a deduction made by an employer which could have the effect of indirectly reducing the minimum wage established by the act. In other words, where an employer felt that he could make deductions indirectly, he would be prevented from doing so by this particular clause.
I should like to refer also to the principle contained in clause 11 of the bill. I had occasion while speaking on a previous bill of a similar nature to take some objection to this type of provision. There is a great tendency to increase the burden of bookkeeping on the employer. We all know that in these days employers are required to do a good deal of bookkeeping for the government of Canada in connection with income tax deductions, workmen's compensation where it applies in the provinces, the deduction and charging of unemployment insurance, making numerous returns and the keeping of a great number of books and records for the government.
So far as this clause imposes on an employer the necessity of setting up and creating a separate set of books merely to indicate that he is paying the minimum wage of $1 an hour, I think it is wrong and I do not agree with it. I think the normal books set up at the present time to comply with the numerous government requirements should be sufficient record to show whether or not an employer is in fact paying his employees the minimum wage, particularly when the bill relates to federal government employees and employees of services and businesses allied with the federal government. In all such cases it must be recognized that fair and complete books are already kept, and I think it is unnecessary to set up any separate or additional bookkeeping system merely to prove that an individual employer is paying the minimum wage provided by the bill.
Of course in clause 12 there is provision for an extension-

Mr. Speaker, if I might speak for a moment on this point which Your Honour has raised, I would point out that the same point was raised previously in connection with another bill on which I was speaking. At that time the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre suggested I should not be able to refer to individual clauses of the bill. After that I took the trouble to look into the question, and if Your Honour would permit me I should like to say a few words on it. I referred to the Canadian books which are available in order to find what has been the actual practice.
I do submit first, Your Honour, that every bill presented to the house is merely a number of clauses, a group of clauses. We cannot merely say this is a bill but there are no clauses in it. In order to establish the principle we have to consider the individual clauses. My understanding of the rule as it has been established by custom in the British houses of parliament and here in the House of Commons is that a member should not be permitted on second reading to discuss the clauses of a bill seriatim-and the word seriatim which I looked up in the dictionary, particularly in Murray's new English dictionary, volume 8, which is to be found in our library, is as follows: "one after another, or one by one in succession."
Mr. Speaker, I should like to suggest that the true statement of this rule is to be found in Bourinot's fourth edition at page 511. This is a Canadian book, and at page 511 it states: On the motion for second reading it is out of order to discuss the clauses seriatim.
I made a particular point, Mr. Speaker, of not discussing the clauses seriatim. I did feel that several of the sections raised individual points and principles which ought to be discussed.

speechtext: I would not go so far as to say that the rule can be circumvented merely by reversing the order of the clauses as the hon. member suggests. I think it is very well understood that the reason for this rule is that in committee we consider each of the clauses separately and the go through the bill considering it clause by clause. But if it is not proper for a member in speaking to pick out a certain clause and say, "There is a principle to be found in this clause and I wish to discuss that principle," then it would be the duty of the Speaker to call the member to order if he felt the member had gone beyond the point of discussing the principle and was merely discussing various clauses. I believe it would be a matter for the Speaker to decide at what point a member was not following the rules and was merely reversing the order, but I do not think going from clause 10 to clause 7 or 8 would necessarily be that.

The second reading of a bill is that stage when it is proper to enter into a discussion and propose a motion relative to the principle of the measure. On the motion for the second reading, it is out of order to discuss the clauses of the bill.

Mr. Speaker, it is a pleasure to rise to speak to a C.C.F. motion with over 20 minutes to go because on three previous occasions when I rose to speak on motions, bills, resolutions and what not, sponsored by hon. gentlemen in that group I had to content myself with observations well within a two minute period, and that of course gave rise to their drawing the unjustifiable inference that I was attempting to talk out their measures. Happily today we have still 22 minutes at our disposal. I will be reasonably brief and there will still be opportunity to vote on the measure which I regard basically as a sound one.
I noticed in the November 1957 issue of Canadian Labour the following paragraphs which are germane to this debate. I am aware, Mr. Speaker, that in quoting them I am repeating what my friend the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre has already quoted, but since the previous debate occurred approximately two months ago perhaps it would be wise to refresh our memories. I am referring to an article dealing with an appearance before the dominion government of the Canadian Labour Congress on October 21, and at page 17 these words occur:
But the dominion should not confine itself to doing as well as the best of the provinces. It should give a lead. It should, specifically, establish a legal maximum work week of 40 hours and a legal minimum wage of $1 an hour. This is not really a very drastic proposal. About 65 per cent of all plant workers in manufacturing now have a standard work week of 40 hours or less. So have all railway workers, and a host of others. The 40-hour week is, indeed, now the predominant practice, and its legal enforcement would merely give a smallish minority of workers what the vast majority already enjoy. As for the minimum wage, there must be precious few workers in industries under dominion jurisdiction who are not getting at least $1 an hour. In some

industries under provincial jurisdiction a minimum of $1 an hour might be hard to apply immediately, but in most provinces the legal minimum rates are preposterously low, and if parliament set a minimum of $1 for industries under its jurisdiction, that might provide a spur to provincial laggards.
I think in the last few lines I quoted we perhaps can find the key to this request of the Canadian Labour Congress, and also the request of the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre, for the legislation that is now being considered and that is a spur to the provincial laggards if such there be. I would hope that if the hon. member does speak later in this debate he would answer this question. Action by this federal parliament would presumably set an example but would it necessarily follow that any provincial laggard would follow that example.
The other day while participating briefly in the debate on the measure concerning the voluntary revocable check-off I had occasion to table some information given me by the economics and research branch of the Department of Labour, which will be found at page 3776 of Hansard. In my opinion the figures set forth there are of importance in this debate. The figures show that there are
413,000	employees under federal jurisdiction. Of these 294,000 operate under some form of agreement, and I presume this means a contract reached as a result of collective bargaining. In other words, 119,000 are not employed under such agreements, and of these some 20,000 are to be found in the employ of steam railways and another 57,500 in the employ of banks.
With regard to the former I would suppose that with the passage of time an aggressive union such as the Canadian brotherhood of railway employees and other transport workers would pick up these strays and bring them within the union.
With regard to the banks, I would seriously doubt whether any bank employee is now paid a rate under $1 an hour. Of course that was not always so. In any event, the blessings of collective bargaining seem to be on their way for bank employees. I understand that already some unionization has occurred in the province of Ontario and that, once established there, unions will move to banks elsewhere. Therefore I would imagine that the figure of 294,000, which was quoted as the number being under some form of agreement-that is, having the right to bargain collectively-has attained the objective of $1 an hour at least. So far as the others are concerned, the number would not be very large indeed who are under a minimum of $1 an hour. I believe that is borne out by the remarks I quoted from the November issue of Canadian Labour.

There is only one other principle of the bill to which I should like to address myself. I am mindful of Your Honour's remarks in connection with the debate which preceded my rising, namely not to get into a discussion of specific clauses, but I should like to refer briefly to clause 4 and then get away from it as quickly as possible. I do that to point out the principle on which I should like to have an answer from the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre. I refer to clause 4(1) and (2). This clause imposes the obligation that the employees be paid a minimum wage. If we can get this bill through committee it might be better to have the obligation made much more positive; that is, that every employer shall pay a minimum wage. Otherwise, if by some mischance a union should reach an agreement with its company and agree to accept under $1 an hour, and that union should be within federal jurisdiction, under this bill it could in effect mean that the union members would be guilty of an offence against this legislation.
As a corollary to that remark I should like also to point out to the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre that there may be a danger in imposing by legislation a policy of minimum wages. I do not think there is any danger in imposing a minimum wage of $1, but I presume that in the flux of time other figures will be substituted from time to time. The danger, as I see it, is that some industry may get into trouble. I am thinking of one example in New Brunswick where the union had to take over control of the plant, in effect become management and employee at the same time, so they could run the business; otherwise the plant would have shut down and dislocated the entire town.
I think there are such examples in different parts of Canada. I realize there are not too many. We are thankful for that, but still there are examples. If the hands of the union were fettered and the union were prevented from entering into an agreement which was best for its purpose-and it might be best for its purpose to include a wage below any minimum set by parliament- then I think you would run into certain dangers in this sort of legislation.
I may have given my friends to understand by my remarks that I am against the legislation. I am not against it, but I did want to raise two or three specific points. My first point is, are we accomplishing anything by setting the provinces an example? My second one is the point I have just made.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, as the representative of the riding of York South, where we have a very large

Industrial Relations
percentage of working people, I rise to lend some measure of support to this bill.
In view of the examples set by the provinces I am surprised to learn that no minimum wage rate has been set by the federal government. It will be noted that under the interpretation section of this bill no distinction is made between male and female workers, which is a change from the provincial act covering this subject. I note that in the Canadian Labour Congress presentation to the cabinet it is pointed out that the maximum legal minimum wage in effect in the provinces is 75 cents for male and 65 cents for female workers.
I do not think anyone is going to quarrel with me when I say that under present-day conditions those minimums are entirely unrealistic. If those standards were in effect a very low standard of living would result. Yet there is a danger, Mr. Speaker, that a minimum wage rate may well become the maximum. There are those in the labour movement who still have doubts as to the wisdom of pressing for this type of legislation. However, this bill does provide a minimum wage of $1 an hour for both sexes, which is the figure adopted by the Canadian Labour Congress, and I assume that all aspects of the matter must have received the consideration of that body.
The explanatory note says:
The purpose ol this bill is to establish a minimum rate of wages with respect to all employees in Canada who come under federal labour jurisdiction. This bill provides that such minimum rate of wages shall be $1 per hour. The bill also provides that its terms do not affect any employee whose 'rate of wages is higher than the minimum established by this legislation.
While this purports to be the principle of the bill, the interpretation does not give any such indication. It merely goes on to say that the employer means any person, firm or corporation, and so forth. It is true that it is all covered in clause 3, which refers to the application of the act, but it does not say that this legislation shall apply only to those undertakings carried on under the legislative authority of the parliament of Canada. I point this out because the rate of $1 an hour might be all right in protected employment, such as the civil service, but it might not be satisfactory in such fields as seasonal employment where a much higher hourly rate might be necessary.
Therefore I feel that in this respect this bill does not altogether provide that those minimum rates shall apply only to all employees under federal labour jurisdiction. There should be some clarification and some insistance that that shall be so. Furthermore, the bill covers a lot of features which I feel

are removed from the minimum wage principle and might well be matters of discussion and bargaining between employer and employee. For instance, there is a reference to the question of board and lodging. I think that has already been provided for in legislation passed by the house during the present session. It has already been taken care of under a separate act. I find that there are very many clauses in the bill which tend in that direction.
I think the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre has included in the bill a lot of things that do not apply solely to minimum wages. It is for that reason I say I can only give the bill a measure of support. I do believe that a minimum wage should be set, but I think that minimum wage should be in accord with existing conditions so that people will be assured a decent living.

maintopic: INDUSTRIAL RELATIONS
subtopic: PROVISION OF MINIMUM RATE OF WAGES FOR EMPLOYEES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise to speak on the bill because I have had a great deal of experience both as a union worker and also as an employer of union men. I have had a great deal of experience with bargaining committees, negotiating committees and boards of arbitration, and also with trying to enforce minimum wage rates in the province of Ontario. As far as the matter of the minimum wage is concerned, I should like to say that I am certainly in favour of minimum wages and of workers getting all they can within reason. But we must remember that in Canada there are three levels of government, municipal, provincial and federal. In my opinion matters having to do with minimum wages are purely and simply provincial matters. After all, it is easy to pass a bill but it is another thing to enforce it.
As I have already said, I have had experience in trying to enforce the industrial standards act of the province of Ontario. If you pass a bill and say that $1 an hour is to be the minimum wage, you will surely find that in a locality where the prevailing rate is higher the prevailing rate will come down to $1. I have had that experience, and I know what I am talking about. If you go into a municipality where the prevailing rate is less than $1 you then have the problem of enforcing it.
In that case it is not the employers who cause the problem, but rather the employees. After all, they will tell you that they live in a free country and that if they want to work for 90 cents an hour they are going to do it. In order to prosecute them you must have access to payrolls and you have to bring them into court. Who is going to do that in this case? I think the only way those

matters can be attended to is by the provincial governments and through the local courts. I think it would be most unfair for us to saddle the provinces at this time with legislation of this kind unless we ourselves intend to enforce it.
As far as the unions are concerned, it is generally considered that minimum wages are not good labour legislation. I think that can be easily proven. In the constituency from which I come there is the most highly unionized city, I think, in the whole of Canada, and it is one of the best cities in which to live. You never hear anybody there talking about minimum wages because the employees all have their own union agreements, and they are carried out not by the government but by the labour organizations themselves.
While I am in favour of legislation to give people the most we can for the services they render, nevertheless I cannot see that a minimum wage for the whole of Canada is something that would be of benefit to the people. It would certainly be legislation that would be very hard to enforce. Again, who am I to say that $1 an hour should be the minimum wage in Newfoundland, some parts of the province of Quebec or Ontario or anywhere? I think all these things bear out the fact that this is really a provincial matter, and I do not feel that I can support such legislation on the federal level. I say that because I know what I am talking about. As I said, I have been connected with unions and workers for a long time and I am quite satisfied that this is not good legislation. May I call it six o'clock.

I did not say it was a frivolous question. I think most of us depend upon the telegraph systems of this country to do an efficient job. We find now, on inquiry, that a member of the staff of Canadian National Telegraphs did not carry out his duty efficiently in this particular case when the 10 telegrams were handed to the company; that is the situation with regard to telegrams.
So far as the various points that were raised in discussion are concerned, Mr. Chairman, I think any extended remarks might better be reserved for second reading of the bill. I shall touch on one or two matters that were raised today in the course of discussion.
The hon. member for Northumberland urged that the payments that are going to the provinces should be earmarked for the municipalities. He was followed by another hon. member in his own party, the member for Charlotte, who contended that there should be no such thing as earmarking. Indeed, he went so far as to suggest that in saying these payments would be helpful in meeting the problem of unemployment, the government was attaching some conditions to these payments. In speaking yesterday, I said, as recorded at page 3851 of Hansard, that the grants are unconditional; that is the position in law, and that is the true essence of the situation.
I draw again to the attention of hon. members of the house that unquestionably much of the benefit of these payments will go to the municipalities. This has been indicated by various provincial governments. Having regard to the fact that municipal governments and provincial governments are very fertile creators of work in this country, we may be sure that this additional assistance to both municipal and provincial levels of government will unquestionably be productive of work.
Then, Mr. Chairman, I was asked concerning the matter from the point of view that there was some unilateral action involved here. That is not the case at all, Mr. Chairman. In proceeding with the Atlantic adjustment grants, we were taking the course which was indicated at the conference in November, which was contemplated by the conference, and which was expected by those at the conference. In the passage I read in my

remarks yesterday from the communique, Mr. Chairman, there are these words:
It was generally agreed that the over-all economic position of the Atlantic provinces is now such-
Now such. I continue:
-as to justify some special grants in aid to the governments of those provinces from the federal government.
I pointed out yesterday that it was so significant at that conference that there was this general measure of recognition of the fact that some special assistance must be provided for the Atlantic provinces. We proceeded, therefore, precisely in the manner that was approved at the conference. The governments of the four Atlantic provinces met with officials representing the federal government and arrived at the formula, and that formula was then translated into the percentages to which I referred yesterday. It then only remained to decide what should be the total sum of money provided for the Atlantic adjustment grants in aggregate. I indicated yesterday also, Mr. Chairman, that that figure was not just taken out of the air. That figure had a definite relationship to the figures that had been under discussion over the previous two years, the kind of figures that had been discussed from the time Premier Flemming first put forward the concrete proposal for the Atlantic adjustment grants.
I made it quite clear yesterday, when asked this question, that on the basis of the formula which Premier Flemming had first put forward, and which was the whole basis of the thinking in relation to the subject of Atlantic adjustment grants at the conference, only four Atlantic provinces would qualify under that formula. Now, that was recognized at the conference. Whatever the future may hold, certainly in regard to the present situation and in regard to anything in the immediately foreseeable future, it is only the four Atlantic provinces that could have justified a claim for special consideration on the basis of the kind of thinking that was back of the formula that Premier Hugh John Flemming put forward, and that found acceptance at the conference.
There has been no unilateral action in regard to the Atlantic adjustment grants. Similarly there has been no unilateral action, in the sense in which that term was used here in debate, as though it were an opprobrious term, in connection with the other part of the measure now under discussion. My hon. friends seek to make something of the fact that this measure evidently had not been worked out in great elaboration long days before. We have been living here through this session in recent weeks hoping

day by day to see some evidence of rapid progress toward conclusion of the business of the session, hoping always that this conference could be reconvened. As the days passed the problems of the provincial governments in relation to their budgets became more and more pressing, and they are very pressing at the present time. There are provincial budgets that are in the course of being reduced to final form while this measure is debated.
We felt therefore that something had to be done in this situation, faced as we were with a prolongation of this present session of parliament and the pressing needs of provincial treasurers in preparing their budgets. It seemed to us the only fair and proper course was for us to ask parliament to give approval to further assistance to the provinces on an interim basis.
I have made it quite clear from the outset that with this interim provision the provinces may count on it for this year, but that does not tie their hands. It ties the federal government's hands with regard to this year but it does not tie the hands of the provinces, and when the conference is resumed there will be full opportunity for discussion of all elements entering into the problem of arriving at fiscal settlements. This measure will, however, bring valuable assistance to the provinces at this very moment; and the need of bringing that form of assistance to the provinces is, in our view, urgent not only in the light of financial problems of the provinces but also in the light of financial problems of the municipal governments, in addition, of course, to the problem of unemployment.
There is one thing I will do my very best to clear up and that has to do with the tables of figures. Here let me say that I will do my utmost to make clear the basis upon which these figures were prepared. I realize from some of the remarks made yesterday and today, when a serious member such as the hon. member for St. Antoine-Westmount spoke in his second contribution to this discussion, that I have not made this matter clear, and if the committee will bear with me I shall do my best to do so now.
All these figures, with which we are now dealing as I indicated yesterday, are prepared on the basis of estimate. I have not, I am sure, given the house to understand that they are exact figures in any respect. The figures which were used on Saturday were figures, as I mentioned yesterday, which were incomplete because the stabilization factor had not been applied to those figures. There are at the present time only two provinces which derive any benefit from the stabilization
Dominion-Provincial Relations payments. Those two provinces are British Columbia and Prince Edward Island.
I am sure hon. members are aware of the fact that the stabilization principle operates as a floor. If the benefits derived by a province from tax yields, plus the equalization payments, do not come up to the figure established on the stabilization basis, then stabilization payments operate as a floor to protect any province from losing any benefit which it had at the conclusion of the previous quinquennial period which ended on March 31, 1957; it acts as a floor. The new formula increases the provincial share of the yield from income taxes from 10 per cent to 13 per cent; in other words, it changes the old 10-9-50 formula to 13-9-50, commencing April 1, 1958. That means that with regard to these two provinces, which were enjoying the benefit of the floor, a portion of this increase went simply to bring the total of their tax yields plus equalization benefits up to the floor.

Mr. Chairman, I do not intend to make a speech; 1 will wait until second reading before doing that. But I do want to say quite plainly that the explanation the minister has just given for his extraordinary miscalculation between Saturday and Monday is the weakest explanation I have ever heard given in this House of Commons.
I say that because for five years I was parliamentary assistant to the minister of finance, and during that period I was able to acquire an intimate knowledge of the very great ability of that department and of the thorough and painstaking way in which the officers of that department approach fiscal problems.
I know, too, that one branch of the department has been dealing with this problem of the dominion-provincial tax agreements for almost 16 years, during which time it has studied almost every conceivable variation which has been put forward by the provinces and the federal government, even the famous axe proposal of Mr. Drew, and they are well aware of the major items in this agreement of which there are just three; tax-sharing, the equalization payments and, third, the stabilization payments.
The stabilization payments were raised mainly because of the demands made by three successive British Columbia premiers, Mr. Hart, Mr. Johnson and Mr. Bennett, and no official of the Department of Finance who ever went through any one of those negotiations would ever forget stabilization. So I say it was not the officers of the Department of Finance who made this miscalculation; it was the minister himself, with his very scanty knowledge of these affairs working, perhaps, in the seventeenth or eighteenth hour of the 18-hour day on which he prides himself, who made this miscalculation.
We would have thought much more of the minister tonight had he stood up and said, "I did it all myself". I say this because once we had seen the table we recognized the 96698-249
Dominion-Provincial Relations careful and competent work which we expect from the officials, and I say the minister is doing no good to the civil service of Canada in trying to pass off his mistake on them, any more than his chief did last week by producing a secret report in the house.
As I say, I have heard some weak explanations during my lifetime, but never before has any minister of the crown stood up and tried by insinuation to unload his errors on his department. You made that error, you and yourself alone; your department, of course, turned out the proper figures. We, of course, have confidence in those latter figures because we know they have been prepared by people who are well versed in these matters. It is going to be very hard, however, to explain to Premier Bennett and Premier Matheson why they were led up the garden path; that they have merely been misled by a mistake made by the Minister of Finance because he works such long hours.

The fact is that it is not a very good way to win the confidence of the country for one who has to deal with these large sums of money to have to admit that he has made mistakes of the kind the Minister of Finance made in connection with this matter.
The minister keeps talking about these two sets of figures-the Saturday set and the Monday set-simply as the figures that were prepared. At no point does he say who prepared either set. I think in all fairness he should tell us. The minister was good enough to supply a number of us yesterday with a mimeographed copy of the table which he asked to have placed on Hansard* Those of us who have such copies recognize the authenticity of the work that was done in preparing this table because of certain initials which appear on the table. I am glad those initials were not placed in Hansard and that the anonymity of the civil servants doing this work was preserved in that way, but I think the minister should not attempt to tell us that it was a group of civil servants who prepared the figures he gave on Saturday.
That is not the only mistake the minister made. Perhaps the mistake he made last Saturday was that of rushing in where angels fear to tread but he made another mistake yesterday which he has now admitted. We learned from him that he forgot to apply the

Dominion-Provincial Relations stabilization aspect of the formula to the figures and that that was the reason the increase for two provinces had to be reduced. Then when we asked for the explanation as to the changes with respect to the other eight provinces he said last night, as recorded at page 3874 of Hansard:
The other eight provinces receive benefit from the fact that British Columbia and Prince Edward Island do not now take their full share by reason of the prior application of the stabilization principle.
I had spent quite a few hours over the weekend refreshing my understanding of this legislation and I began to wonder if I could be as lacking in intelligence as I had to be if that statement by the minister was correct. As I understand it, the 10 per cent represents that portion of the personal income tax collected by the federal government from residents within the provinces which, by virtue of this legislation, is returned to each province. If you change that 10 per cent to 13 per cent you do not by that process simply arrive at a total sum of $62 million which is given to one group of provinces or the other. I came to the realization last night that if I understood the act at all-and I think it has now been admitted that my understanding of it is not too bad- what we have across the way is a Minister of Finance who does not understand it.

The Minister of Finance takes quite a different attitude on that side of the house from the attitude he adopted when on this


side of the house. He presents a real study in political metamorphosis. When he was on this side of the house and a mistake was made on the other side of the house it was a sin of the worst type. Now it has all been changed. The Minister of Finance admits that telegrams were sent out but that two of the provincial premiers did not receive the telegrams. It .is regrettable; but it was a mistake on the part of an employee of the Canadian National Telegraphs. I resent that, Mr. Chairman. The mistake was on the part of this government in relying on a unilateral method of sending telegrams as a means of consulting the provincial premiers on a matter of such importance as this.
It should not have been dealt with other than by means of a conference. The premiers should have been called back to Ottawa even if all the government was going to do at a resumed session was tell the provincial premiers to their faces what this government was going to do. But, no, the government chose this distinctly unilateral method of sending out telegrams. They were not even telegrams that asked for replies and the government did not check to see if they were received. The minister has admitted that two provincial premiers, the premier of my province of Manitoba, and the premier of Saskatchewan, did not receive their telegrams. They learned about this through what they read in the newspapers. We have the experience of the provincial premiers learning one thing from what they read in the newspapers as a result of Saturday's announcement and learning something else from what they read in the newspapers as a result of Monday's table. I suggest that perhaps some more telegrams are necessary. Some of the provincial premiers may be still wondering just what are going to be the results of this legislation when it is passed.
The Minister of Finance finds it extremely easy to make these explanations that are satisfactory to him. He offers an explanation and that is it; we are supposed to accept his explanation. He made a mistake and forgot the stabilization aspect of the formula. He worked it out on Saturday on the basis of the 1956-57 estimates upped by 5 per cent. His officials decided it would be far better to work out these estimates on the basis of the 1957-58 experience. It is just a coincidence that the two totals are close to each other, in one case $62,203,000 and in the other $62,206,000; but here we have the minister playing around with these figures. He admits himself that the provincial treasurers are in the process of preparing their budgets and it is important to them to know what they will receive under this arrangement and yet he deals with them in this slipshod manner,

a manner which I say certainly does not win the confidence ot the provincial governments or the people of Canada, the kind of confidence that we have to have in the person who presides over this country's federal treasury.
The minister keeps on saying that this was not unilateral action. We are certainly receiving a lesson in argument by assertion. The Minister of Finance, the Hon. Donald M. Fleming, says it is not unilateral. That is it; we must accept it. Take it or leave it.

When the conference met last November it was stated by the Prime Minister that it was the intention to meet briefly and to lay nothing before it but to listen to what the provincial premiers had to say, to consider the whole matter in the light of what they said and then meet again early in the new year to discuss what would be done. There was an agreed communique to which reference has been made a number of times by the Minister of Finance, particularly to one paragraph that he likes to quote. But the following is the last sentence of that agreed communique:
It was agreed that a subsequent meeting be held as soon as possible in the new year in accordance with the proposal made by the dominion government in calling this conference.
There is no proviso there saying that it would not be done if the session of parliament lasted too long. It was a clear understanding on the part of the ten provincial premiers and the Prime Minister that the conference would meet again early in the new year. It was also said in this agreed communique, if I may go back to the penultimate paragraph:
Possible changes in the tax sharing arrangements act were discussed but it was understood that no endeavour would be made to reach conclusions on this matter prior to further consideration of the subject by the dominion government in the light of the public statements made by the provincial representatives in open sessions and the discussions which took place in committee.
The Minister of Finance knows that shortly after that conference was over Premier Campbell of Manitoba wrote the Prime Minister of Canada a letter telling him that his government was not satisfied with the atmosphere of insistence on the part of the Prime Minister in which the provincial premiers were more or less forced to come to an agreement and that there were certain changes that he felt the government should consider before reaching a decision as to the basis of the grants to the Atlantic provinces and on any other changes in the tax sharing 96698-249i
Dominion-Provincial Relations arrangements act. Through all of that correspondence it was crystal clear that there was to be another meeting in January of the federal-provincial conference. When the Prime Minister came into this house the day after the conference was over and referred to the agreed communique and tabled it in the house and told us about the conference, he said in his concluding sentence as recorded at page 1556 of Hansard of November 27, 1957:
A subsequent meeting as soon as possible in the new year will be held in accordance with the proposals made by this government in calling the conference.
The Prime Minister was talking to the House of Commons. No suggestion was made by him that this would have to be changed if the parliamentary session did not come to a conclusion at a date satisfactory to the government. I have already referred, as have other hon. members, to the correspondence exchanged between Premier Campbell and the Prime Minister of Canada. It is really a one-sided correspondence because the only letter of any length was that written by Premier Campbell on December 18. In that letter Premier Campbell, after discussing all the angles of this matter in a very commendable manner, said this:
If we are able to have this information in advance, Manitoba will be better prepared to discuss the final special Atlantic arrangements which we understand you are planning to put forward for general consideration and acceptance at the next meeting of the adjourned dominion-provincial conference in January of 1958.
This was Mr. Campbell's clear understanding, namely that there was to be a meeting in January of 1958 and he asked for consideration of his letter so those concerned would be in a position to discuss these matters when the premiers came back here in January. The letter continues:
If all the provinces are similarly informed of the adjustment formula being considered for the Atlantic provinces,-
Of course, they were all informed last Saturday, those who got the telegrams, that the matter was settled.
-our January meeting could more surely and quickly deal with the final disposition of this matter which has great importance to our friends in the Atlantic provinces now, and which may well have even greater long-term significance for other parts of Canada as well.
Yours sincerely,
Douglas Campbell.
That is the letter that Premier Campbell wrote to the Prime Minister on December 18, and in which he made it clear that it was his understanding, on the basis of the communique and on the basis of what was said at the conference, that they would be meeting

Dominion-Provincial Relations again in January. What was the Prime Minister's reply to that letter? It was as follows: Ottawa, December 21, 1957.
My dear Premier:
On my return from attending the NATO council meetings in Paris, I have received your letter of December 18 in regard to the discussion which took place at the recent dominion-provincial conference.
This is only an interim acknowledgement of your letter. My colleagues and I will wish to study carefully your further submission before commenting on it. I shall merely assure you that this matter will receive our careful attention.
Yours sincerely,
John G. Diefenbaker.
I have read the entire letter that the Prime Minister wrote to Premier Campbell. I want to come back to the substance of that letter in a moment, but I read it now to make it clear that the Prime Minister did not in any way challange Premier Campbell's statement in his letter that it was expected that they would meet in January of this year. In other words, Mr. Chairman, it was clearly understood-indeed, this was in the nature of a promise-that they would be called together again to deal with this matter. But despite many questions which we have asked and letters from other premiers, the month has just about gone by without that conference being held.
May I now come back again, Mr. Chairman,-just in order to show how unilateral this action is-to the way in which the premier of my province has been treated. Some of us will try to give him a certain kind of treatment later on this year, but at the moment he is the premier of Manitoba, trying to represent the interests of that province so far as federal-provincial arrangements are concerned.

With
the support of Premier Douglas and one or two others he is doing a very good job.
On January 13 I asked the Prime Minister whether he had replied to Premier Campbell's letter of December 18. When I asked the Prime Minister on January 13 whether he had yet replied, this was his answer as reported at page 3245 of Hansard:
I shall be obliged to look up the letters in question before I am in a position to answer.
Frankly, Mr. Chairman, I do not regard as a sample of very close attention to this important matter the fact that on January

13 the Prime Minister did not know whether or not he had answered Premier Campbell's important letter of December 18. Mr. Speaker, I have not had any opportunity to consider that matter since the hon. gentleman asked the question. But, Mr. Chairman, on Saturday of that week we were informed by the Minister of Finance, not that a letter had gone to Premier Campbell answering the lengthy and substantial case that he made on December 18 but rather that "take it or leave it" telegrams had been sent to the ten provincial premiers telling them what was going to be done. On January 25, Mr. Chairman, the day on which the Minister of Finance told us about these telegrams, I made a further reference to Premier Campbell's letter in these words which are found at page 3796 of Hansard of January 25:
Will there be any other reply by letter to Premier Campbell of Manitoba with respect to the letter he wrote the Prime Minister on December 18, in which he discussed the whole question of the relationship between changes for all the provinces and special grants for the Atlantic provinces, or will further discussion of Premier Campbell's suggestions be left until the federal-provincial conference is reconvened?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: DOMINION-PROVINCIAL RELATIONS MEASURE TO PROVIDE FINANCIAL ASSISTANCE TO ATLANTIC PROVINCES, ETC.
speechtext:
I had better not speak too positively without refreshing my memory on the contents of Premier Campbell's letter, but 1 think it will be clear that the course of action proposed by the government as indicated in the telegram is a fairly complete course of action with regard to the immediate situation. Broader questions can best be considered when the dominion-provincial conference reconvenes.
There it is, Mr. Chairman. On January 13 the Prime Minister did not know whether or not he had answered Premier Campbell's letter. On January 20 he said it was his intention to answer it. On January 25 the Minister of Finance says there will not be any other answer than this telegram to Premier Campbell, and that these broader questions that he has raised can be dealt with at the next meeting of the dominion-provincial conference. Yet the Minister of

Finance has the gall to stand up here tonight and to say that this government is not acting unilaterally in this matter.
I know that hon. members opposite find it difficult to understand that we are speaking critically of the government in relation to a piece of legislation that we are going to support. We have made that clear on this side of the house right from the start, that the provinces need this money and that we feel particularly that the Atlantic provinces should have the assistance that is envisaged in this legislation. But as my hon. friends opposite must remember from the days when they were on this side of the house that it is important not only to get things done but to do things in the right way; and the right way to deal with federal-provincial relationships is to deal with them on a basis of co-operation, consultation and of mutual knowledge and understanding as to what is going on. That is what this government has failed to do. They are flying in the face of all the language that the Minister of Finance, the Prime Minister and Mr. Drew used in 1956, when they characterized what the Liberals were doing as being one-sided, unilateral, as inflexible as the laws of the Medes and Persians and so on.
I call upon the Minister of Finance and the government not again to make the mistake that the minister made of doing his own arithmetic, of bringing in statements which are incorrect, of answering questions without knowing how this legislation operates. I call upon them also not again to deal with any matter of federal-provincial relationships without doing it on a basis of conference, consultation and full understanding between the federal government and the provinces.
The minister says this is on an interim basis only; that the hands of the provinces are not tied so far as the 1958-59 fiscal year is concerned. He says that the federal government's hands are tied, that they will have to pay out this money but that the provinces are not tied. He knows that "interim" can be a long time. I think somewhere in the book of Genesis there is a verse that got missed where Adam said to Eve as they were going out of the garden, "My dear, we are in an age of transition".
A temporary or interim period can last a long time, especially when the provinces are waiting for the federal government to reconvene this conference. The months of the 1958-59 fiscal year will add up one after another-seriatim, for the benefit of my friend the hon. member for Parry Sound-Muskoka-and by the time the conference does meet again the year will be so far gone that the discussions will have to relate to the
Dominion-Provincial Relations next year and not to this one. This is not a way to assist the provinces materially or effectively so far as their 1958-59 needs are concerned.
I make just one other comment, Mr. Chairman, and it is this. The 1956 legislation brought down by the former government, which this government is now accepting in principle right down the line, had one important thing wrong with it. We pointed this out at the time even though we voted for the legislation because we felt there had to be a continuance of federal-provincial sharing of tax revenues. But in our view the one thing that was wrong with the legislation when it was brought down was that it did not take into account the fiscal needs of provinces or areas. The so-called principle of equalization which is good, does not go that far. We feel that changes should yet be made in this legislation to recognize, as some of the previous agreements did to a certain extent, the principle of fiscal need. We are disappointed that the government does not seem to be facing up to that need and does not seem even to be giving us the assurance that the principle of equalization brought in by the Liberals will be continued without being interfered with in any way.
Therefore, Mr. Chairman, the government across the way has a great deal yet to learn about proper and adequate federal-provincial fiscal arrangements and it has a great deal to learn about co-operation and consultation, about following a course that will really keep relations between Ottawa and the provinces on a healthy basis.

Mr. Chairman, this afternoon I asked a number of questions based on the figures tabled yesterday by the Minister of Finance. I think that questions dealing with figures should be dealt with at the resolution stage when we are in committee because first of all the figures are tabled during the discussion in committee and, second, in spite of the suggestion made by the Minister of Finance a few moments ago I do not believe it is possible to discuss figures in the same way on second reading and therefore it should be done in committee.
I am going to repeat one of the questions I asked this afternoon which is based on the figures found in the table. speechtext:
My hon. friend knows quite well, and no member of this house knows better than he does, that when you bring a reduction into effect it does take time to work out the revisions in the tables of deductions. Most of the people in this country pay their income tax on the basis of deductions from wages and salary, and when reductions are brought about no government that has been created yet can bring those deductions into effect and have the tables all ready to put the rates of deduction into effect at once.
When we brought in a reduction in the income tax in December, it was made clear then that we would expedite, by every means in our power, the establishment of new rates of deductions, new tables, so that they would be in the hands of all persons who are charged with the duty of making these deductions. We are going to do the same thing here. Just as soon as it is possible to arrive at the revised tables of deduction in Quebec, they will be made available. In the case of any who, in advance of receiving the new revised tables of deductions, have paid at the old rate, they will be entitled to reduce their payments accordingly. If at the end of the year there is any over-payment they are, according to well established practice, entitled to a refund.

speechtext:
the second reading of Bill No. 170, to implement an agreement between Canada and Australia for the avoidance of double taxation with respect to income tax.
He said: Mr. Speaker, the purpose of this bill is to give legal effect in Canada to the agreement which, as a result of negotiations and subsequent exchanges, has been reached between the government of Canada and the government of Australia for the avoidance of double taxation of income. This agreement was signed at Mont Tremblant on October 1, 1957.
The provisions of this agreement are similar in their general effect to those contained in the agreements which Canada has made with the United States, the United Kingdom, Sweden, New Zealand, Ireland, Denmark, Germany, South Africa and The Netherlands.
Double taxation is to be avoided mainly by means of reciprocal tax credits according to which the country of residence gives credit for the tax imposed by the country in which the income has its source.
The extent of possible double taxation is also reduced by a reduction or binding of the rates of withholding taxes imposed at the source on certain income going abroad. On dividends the Australian rates are reduced from a maximum of 40 per cent to 15 per cent while the Canadian rate remains at 15 per cent.
As in the other agreements, taxation of the trading profits of an enterprise is limited to those profits attributable to the permanent establishment of such an enterprise. Thus, casual profits earned by companies in selling goods in a country where they have no fixed place of business are not taxed by that country. Similarly, certain specific provisions restrict the taxation of profits from the operation of ships and aircraft to the country of residence of the operator and the taxation of the remuneration of exchange teachers to the country of their normal residence.
The agreement also provides for the exchange of information upon request.
The agreement is effective, for Canadian tax, commencing with the taxation year in which the agreement comes into force, and

Dominion Succession Duty Act for Australian tax, commencing with the year of income-July 1 to June 30-in which the agreement comes into force. The agreement will come into force when the act is proclaimed by the governor in council. The agreement continues in force until March 31, 1960, and indefinitely thereafter unless notice of termination is given.
Motion agreed to, bill read the second time, considered in committee and reported.

Ottawa, Canada.
My dear Prime Minister:
I am enclosing copy of my letter to Premier Campbell in connection with dominion-provincial matters.
As you will note it deals with some of the implications raised in his letter to you under date of December 18th.
My letter is more or less self-explanatory and is intended to make plain New Brunswick's natural concern that the matter of special adjustment grants to the Atlantic provinces should not become involved once again in the question of dominion-provincial relationships in general. Such discussions can only mean further delay for assistance which is urgently needed.
My letter also emphasizes the fact, upon which we place particular stress, that our economic disabilities have existed for generations and are not merely the result of some economic fluctuation. The chronic character of our difficulties has, of course, been repeatedly recognized by royal commissions
and other authorized bodies investigating conditions over the years.
With all good wishes for 1958.
Yours sincerely,
Hugh John Flemming
THE PREMIER Fredericton
December 27th, 1957.
Honourable Douglas Campbell,
Premier,
Province of Manitoba,
Winnipeg, Manitoba.
Dear Mr. Campbell:
I acknowledge your letter of December 20th in regard to dominion-provincial affairs and also the copy of your letter to the Prime Minister under date of December 18th last.
I have read this correspondence with great care and, while appreciating the features of Manitoba's position as set forth, I cannot help but feel concerned about the possible influence of your suggestions to the Prime Minister upon the general interests of the Atlantic provinces. I believe that this could be very unfavourable at such a critical time in the history of the relationship of the governments in this region with the national government. It is certainly our hope and, I feel, of all four governments in the region, that our special situation can be expeditiously dealt with in the manner presently being proposed by the government of Canada.
It seems to me that the significant and unique character of the situation of the Atlantic provinces resides in the protracted duration of economic disability. All provinces are subject to economic fluctuation and some more than others, but the compelling fact of our situation is that for generations our development has consistently and chronically lagged far behind the general growth of Canada. It is the extent and degree of this long term retardation which creates our special problem.
I shall be glad if you will accord these views your customary courteous and thoughtful consideration, and I am most grateful for your personal courtesy in keeping me informed.
In view of the circumstances, I am sending a copy of this letter to the Prime Minister and to the premiers of the other Atlantic provinces.
Yours sincerely,
Hugh John Flemming
Wednesday, January 29, 1958
